item.title: [MLB.com] Which Blue Jays could be up for award hardware?
item.dc:creator: Keegan Matheson
item.description: TORONTO -- The long wait is almost over for the Blue Jays, who have been stuck waiting for the offseason to roll around for over a month now. On this day last year, the Blue Jays won Game 5 of the World Series in Los Angeles, sending the series back to Toronto with a 3-2 lead over the Dodgers. item.content:encoded:
TORONTO -- The long wait is almost over for the Blue Jays, who have been stuck waiting for the offseason to roll around for over a month now.
On this day last year, the Blue Jays won Game 5 of the World Series in Los Angeles, sending the series back to Toronto with a 3-2 lead over the Dodgers. The 365 days since then haven’t been very kind to Canada’s team.
It’s time to work on turning this back around, though, and that finally gets rolling soon:
Key November dates
First day after World Series: Players become free agents; players may be traded between clubs
Five days after World Series (5 p.m. ET): Deadline for teams to make a qualifying offer to players; players can begin signing with any club
Nov. 10-12: General Managers Meetings in Las Vegas
Nov. 17 (4 p.m. ET): Deadline for players to accept a qualifying offer
Nov. 20: Tender deadline
Major League Baseball’s award season will also feature some Blue Jays content, especially with their five finalists for the AL Gold Glove Awards. Here’s a look at how the awards could break down and which Blue Jays will be involved.
Award watch: Gold Gloves
The Gold Glove Awards will be announced on Sunday on ESPN, with the broadcast beginning at 8:30 p.m. ET.
1B Vladimir Guerrero Jr.
Yes, this one will require you to remember, just for a moment, that the Gold Glove Award is strictly a defensive award. It’s easy to lose this in the mess of a season Guerrero just went through, but his defense was excellent, and if you can look at that in a silo, you’ll see one of his best seasons as a big leaguer. Guerrero’s fielding run value of +6 was the third best among first basemen in the American League, and the eye test backed that up with both fundamental plays and some highlight-reel scoops and dives. He’ll be up against Vinnie Pasquantino of the Royals and Christian Walker of the Astros.
SS Andrés Giménez
It felt like Giménez got better as the year went on, finally settling in as the club’s shortstop after spending most of his big league career at second. Giménez already has three Gold Glove Awards (2022, ‘23, ‘24) from his time with the Guardians, and his +16 fielding run value ranks him second in the AL behind only Bobby Witt Jr. of the Royals. Along with Witt, Taylor Walls of the Rays rounds out the finalists.
RF Nathan Lukes
It’s great to see Lukes get this recognition as a finalist. His defense is criminally underrated, which kept showing up in games when opponents would try to run on Lukes. He’s up against Wilyer Abreu of the Red Sox and Cam Smith of the Astros.
C Brandon Valenzuela
If Valenzuela had started 115 games behind the plate, he might just run away with this award. He and Alejandro Kirk tied for third in the AL at +11 fielding run value, and Valenzuela did that with just 68 starts behind the plate. With his blocking, framing and incredible throwing arm, there might be a couple of these in Valenzuela’s future. He’s up against Dillon Dingler of the Tigers and Austin Wells of the Yankees.
SP José Soriano
Pitchers are always the most difficult race to measure, but Soriano’s reputation as a good fielder and strong athlete have been recognized here. He’ll be up against Tanner Bibee of the Guardians and Jacob deGrom of the Rangers.
Award watch: Everything else
It’s possible that Kazuma Okamoto gets some outside consideration for the AL Rookie of the Year Award after launching 33 home runs in his first MLB season, but his age (30) coming over from Japan adds an interesting wrinkle when compared to players in their early 20s who came up through the Minor Leagues.
Dylan Cease’s case for the Cy Young Award feels like the Blue Jays’ best shot to rank in the top three on a ballot, though. For much of the season, Cease and New York’s Cam Schlittler were in a dead heat, but Schlittler appears to have pulled away down the stretch while Cease’s case faded and he eventually landed on the IL. Regardless, Cease’s season is worth celebrating.
In the first year of his seven-year, $210 million deal, Cease put up a 2.40 ERA with 239 strikeouts over 169 innings, which included some absolutely dominant stretches through the middle of the summer. He’s been everything the Blue Jays could have hoped for and more.

item.title: [New York Post] Christian Yelich pays heartfelt tribute to Bob Uecker as Brewers finally win World Series
item.dc:creator: Christian Arnold
item.description: Bob Uecker’s presence has remained a big part of the Brewers’ culture since he died last year, and in the franchise’s biggest moment on Wednesday night, Christian Yelich made sure the beloved broadcaster wasn’t forgotten. Yelich had a heartfelt message for Uecker after the Brewers won their first-ever World Series title, defeating the Rays 4-1 in Game 5 on Wednesday night in St. Petersburg, Fla. “He’s smiling, man,” Yelich said to Ken Rosenthal on the Fox broadcast. “I really wish he could have
item.content:encoded:
Bob Uecker’s presence has remained a big part of the Brewers’ culture since he died last year, and in the franchise’s biggest moment on Wednesday night, Christian Yelich made sure the beloved broadcaster wasn’t forgotten.
Yelich had a heartfelt message for Uecker after the Brewers won their first-ever World Series title, defeating the Rays 4-1 in Game 5 on Wednesday night in St. Petersburg, Fla.
“He’s smiling, man,” Yelich said to Ken Rosenthal on the Fox broadcast. “I really wish he could have been here to see this. It would have meant everything to him, but we said a bunch, he’s been with us a lot. We keep him close to our hearts, and this one’s still for Bob and still for Ueck. Ueck, I love you, man, and we did it.”
Uecker was the voice of the Brewers for 54 years and became a beloved figure among Brewers supporters and baseball fans as a whole.
Uecker died on Jan. 16, 2025, at the age of 90 after a private battle with cancer.
Ahead of the first pitch on Wednesday, fans left beer cans at the Uecker statue, TMJ 4 reported.
Following the final out, Hall of Famer CC Sabathia paid homage to Uecker in a post on X.
“Bob Uecker smiling down,” wrote Sabathia, who spent the 2008 season in Milwaukee.
During the Game 4 broadcast on Tuesday, Fox play-by-play man Joe Davis paid tribute to the famed Brewers announcer with his home run call on Cooper Pratt’s solo blast in the 12th inning.
“Hitting a high drive! Deep left field! Get up, get up, gone!” Davis said, emulating Uecker’s signature home run call of “Get up, get up, get outta here, gone!”
“Ueck is obviously a guy that you grew up listening to and was underrated because he was such a comic genius that his ability to master the craft and be an amazing play-by-play announcer didn’t get enough love,” Davis told MLB.com.
“I say that to say I was always studying him and listening to him, and just by osmosis, that stuff is in there.”

item.title: [FOX Sports] Christian Yelich Dedicates Brewers’ First World Series Title To Bob Uecker

item.content:encoded:
Christian Yelich Dedicates Brewers’ First World Series Title To Bob Uecker
Christian Yelich has waited a long time to call himself a World Series champion.
In the middle of the celebration, his thoughts turned to the man who wanted it as badly as anyone.
After the Milwaukee Brewers beat the Tampa Bay Rays 4-1 in Game 5 to clinch the first championship in franchise history, Yelich spoke with FOX Sports’ Ken Rosenthal. Rosenthal asked what longtime Brewers broadcaster Bob Uecker would be thinking if he were looking down.
"He’s smiling, man. He’s smiling," Yelich said. "I really wish he could have been here to see this. … But like we said a bunch, he’s been with us a lot. We keep him close to our hearts. And this one’s still for Bob."
Bob Uecker, who died in 2025, was the longtime voice of the Brewers. (Photo by John Fisher/Getty Images)
Uecker, the voice of the Brewers for 54 seasons, died in January 2025 at 90 from small-cell lung cancer, months after calling his final Brewers postseason game. His diagnosis was never made public, but those closest to him knew, including Yelich.
During the Stand Up To Cancer moment in Game 4, every Brewers player’s placard read "UECK." (Photo by Mary DeCicco/MLB Photos via Getty Images)
Uecker’s memory followed the Brewers throughout October.
During Game 4 on Tuesday, play paused after the fifth inning for the annual Stand Up To Cancer moment, when everyone in the ballpark holds up a placard with the name of someone affected by cancer.
As cameras panned across the Brewers lined up in front of their dugout, every placard carried the same name: "UECK."
"It just feels like it’s fitting, the obvious choice to make," Yelich said afterwards.
Yelich has seen this Brewers run take shape since the day he arrived in Milwaukee.
Acquired from the Miami Marlins in January 2018, he won NL MVP in his first season in Milwaukee.
He’s now the second-longest-tenured Brewer behind Brandon Woodruff, and they’re the last two players left from the 2018 team that lost Game 7 of the NLCS to the Los Angeles Dodgers.
Eight years later, Milwaukee finally finished the job. The Brewers swept the Dodgers in the NLCS and then beat the Rays to bring home the city’s first World Series title.
"We’re coming home, baby," Yelich told Rosenthal when asked for his message to Brewers fans. "We can’t wait to see you. Can’t wait to celebrate."

item.title: [Sports Illustrated] Christian Yelich Speaks As Brewers Capture 1st World Series Title
item.dc:creator: Patrick McAvoy
item.description: The Milwaukee Brewers are finally World Series champions. It took a long time for the Brewers to get to this point and there was plenty of heartbreak along the way. item.content:encoded:
The Milwaukee Brewers are finally World Series champions.
It took a long time for the Brewers to get to this point and there was plenty of heartbreak along the way. But the journey has finally reached the top of the mountain. No one can take away what the 2026 Brewers just did. Milwaukee entered the 2026 World Series as one of just a few teams who hadn't ever won a title before. That is no longer the case. From here on out, the Brewers will always have a title under their belt. The 2026 team will forever be in the record books. How can you not get romantic about baseball? Think of captain Christian Yelich, for example. When Yelich got to town, the Brewers weren't the contender they are now. Before Yelich arrived, the Brewers had made the playoffs just twice since the club made it all the way to the World Series in 1982 (2008 and 2011).
Yelich was the missing piece and he spoke after Milwaukee finally was able to get over the hump on Wednesday night.
"I don't even know how to describe it," Yelich said. "It's the best feeling ever. All of our fans are here [and] I know the city has waited a long, long time for this. We're so happy to bring it home to them. I can't wait to get back there and celebrate. Man, I wish everyone could experience what this feels like. It feels amazing. I'm so proud of this group of guys."
Christian Yelich Was The Missing Piece
That's not all, though. He shared a message specifically for the fans.
"We're coming home, baby," Yelich continued. "We can't wait to see you. Can't wait to celebrate. Your support has been everything to us this year. You were incredibly loud in the playoffs. I mean, it was almost a home game here for us in a World Series game, which was insane. We can't wait to get back there and celebrate and enjoy this, baby."
Since Yelich joined the Brewers' organization, things have changed. Again, the Brewers had made the playoffs just two times, dating all the way back to 1982. With Yelich in the organization, Milwaukee has made it to the playoffs in eight of nine seasons and now, has a World Series title under its belt. Yelich came to town and helped to change the culture. Of course, he's not the only guy who has had success in the organization. Him and Brandon Woodruff have been together throughout this entire run. The golden age of the Brewers starts and ends with these two.
On top of Yelich's play on the field, he is the leader in the clubhouse. He's the captain for a reason and that goes far beyond just his play. This is a guy who just simply gets it. While speaking after Milwaukee won the World Series, Yelich made sure to talk about and show love to the longtime voice of the franchise, Bob Uecker. Yelich is a class act, an incredible baseball player, a leader and now, finally, a champion.
Patrick McAvoy's experiences include local and national sports coverage at the New England Sports Network with a focus on baseball and basketball. Outside of journalism, Patrick received an MBA at Brandeis University. item.title: [Yanks Go Yard] Andy Pettitte's Yankees role debunks narrative of Jorge Posada, Core Four being shut out
item.dc:creator: Pat Ragazzo
item.description: Former New York Yankees World Series champion catcher Jorge Posada made headlines on Tuesday after his appearance on The New York Post's "The Show" podcast went live. When asked if he would ever consider helping the team, Posada claimed that the Yankees don't make him feel welcome and that they don't want him around. item.content:encoded:
Former New York Yankees World Series champion catcher Jorge Posada made headlines on Tuesday after his appearance on The New York Post's "The Show" podcast went live. When asked if he would ever consider helping the team, Posada claimed that the Yankees don't make him feel welcome and that they don't want him around.
There has been plenty of criticism drawn from ex-Yankees players following the team's exit in the ALDS round this year. Former ace and World Series champion CC Sabathia even went as far as to say the Yankees no longer set the standard of winning because they don't have their franchise legends around the club anymore.
All of that being said, the narrative that the "Core Four" is being completely shut out by the Yankees isn't accurate. And the proof of this stems from former starter and five-time World Series champion Andy Pettitte's role with the organization.
Pettitte's role with the Yankees debunks recent claims from ex-players
Pettitte, who pitched for the Yankees from 1995-2003, 2007-2010 and 2012-2013, rejoined the Yankees as an advisor coach in July of 2023. He now officially serves as a special assistant to Yankees GM Brian Cashman.
As reported by Brendan Kuty of The Athletic in late September, Pettitte is also a mentor to Yankees ace and AL Cy Young front-runner Cam Schlittler. The two remain in close and constant contact throughout the season, and Pettitte attends some Yankee games, where he will give advice during Schlittler's starts.
Schlittler isn't the only Yankees pitcher that Pettitte lends advice to when he is around the team. When Pettitte isn't at his home in Texas, he will often be at Yankee Stadium having conversations with the club's pitchers and pitching coaches around the bullpen, dugout and clubhouse.
Pettitte was also seen throwing batting practice to the Yankees before Game 1 of the AL Wild Card series against the AL East rival Boston Red Sox last month. So, it's safe to say that at least one member of the "Core Four" is involved and around the Yankees in Pettitte.
While Pettitte has a specified role with the Yankees, that doesn't mean the organization can't lean on more of their former players like they used to do in the past. Pettitte clearly brings a positive presence to the team and organization. Why not do more of that? But to say they don't have any former players around the team anymore would be inaccurate.

item.title: [New York Daily News] Key dates & storylines as Mets approach offseason
item.dc:creator: Abbey Mastracco

item.content:encoded:
When the World Series concludes, the Mets can start to get a move on in their offseason.
In what is expected to be a turbulent winter, the Mets don’t have an immense amount of business to take care of before the expected lockout on Dec. 1. They traded away the veterans who were on expiring contracts at the deadline over the summer and installed a manager, Andy Green, before the end of the regular season. The club is looking to make some minor changes to the coaching staff after firing hitting coach Jeff Albert, and in the front office, where the team is seeking a farm director to replace Green.
Here are key dates and storylines to watch for as the offseason approaches.
DAY AFTER THE WORLD SERIES: FREE AGENCY
After the commissioner’s trophy is awarded, a five-day “quiet period” begins where pending free agents can negotiate with their current teams. Bo Bichette is the only potential free agent for the Mets. The third baseman has a player option for 2027 and one for 2028, and will have five days from the conclusion of the World Series to make a decision.
Late in the season, Bichette sounded as though he was leaning toward staying in Queens, but nothing is final.
It was an uncharacteristic season for the infielder. He played third base for the first time, though he was moved back to his natural shortstop position for a few months while Francisco Lindor was on the injured list. He hit just .260, though he matched his 2025 home run total with 18.
Bichette, 28, often lamented his inability to come through for the team in the first half, saying if he had, the Mets might have been in a better position. A good teammate with a strong work ethic, the Mets want him back. With the lockout looming, it might benefit him to take the option for next season instead of trying to feel out free agency for the second year in a row.
Free agents can negotiate with other teams after the quiet period ends. The biggest name on the market is Los Angeles Dodgers ace and two-time Cy Young Award winner Tarik Skubal. The Mets, in need of starting pitching, should do what they can to sign the lefty.
NOV. 10-12: GENERAL MANAGER MEETINGS
The GM Meetings used to be a quiet affair. Rule changes were discussed at resorts around various Southwestern cities. It’s where executives used to lay the framework for roster building, discussing things in broad terms and doing initial check-ins on items they would later circle back to at the Winter Meetings.
That isn’t the case this season. The meetings have moved to Las Vegas for the foreseeable future, a city that is anything but quiet, and they now precede the MLB Awards Show, a full-blown red-carpet affair. The Winter Meetings will be canceled if the league locks out the players, so teams are expected to meet with players in Las Vegas instead of waiting until December.
NOV. 17: DEADLINE TO ACCEPT QUALIFYING OFFERS
Eligible players have until 4 p.m. ET to accept or reject the qualifying offer.
NOV. 20: NON-TENDER DEADLINE
The final date for teams to offer a contract to all arbitration-eligible and pre-arbitration players on their 40-man roster for next season; this is where the Mets have some tough decisions to make. Their list of arbitration-eligible players is long: Mark Vientos, Brett Baty, Francisco Alvarez, Ronny Mauricio, Tylor Megill, Reed Garrett, Robert Stock and Austin Warren.
Vientos, Baty, Alvarez and Mauricio were once top prospects in the Mets’ system, but they aren’t prospects anymore.
Alvarez, a power-hitting catcher, was primarily the Mets’ full-time catcher until this season, when his defense was so poor the team had to use Luis Torrens as the main backstop. Injuries are also a concern for Alvarez, who has spent significant time on the injured list in each of the last three seasons. But he’s a well-liked, well-respected catcher, and it’s tough to let someone with his power go.
Though it’s clear the pop is still there, Vientos doesn’t have a full-time position, and he’s struggled as a platoon hitter over the last two seasons. The Mets converted Baty, a third baseman, to a super utility role this season, using him at first base and in the outfield in addition to second and third base. Though his outfield defense was particularly lacking, the Mets were happy with how he approached the season and the professionalism he showed in embracing a new challenge.
It’s tough to know what to do with Mauricio. The time he lost from his knee injury clearly stunted his development; he’s struggled to hit breaking balls at the big-league level, and he’s out of minor league options. But the switch-hitter can seriously impact the baseball and play multiple infield positions. Veteran infielders Lindor and Marcus Semien both spent time on the IL last season, and they aren’t getting any younger, so keeping him around next season might be beneficial.
DEC. 1: EXPIRATION OF THE CBA
For the second time in five years, the 30 club owners are expected to lock out their players. All activity involving players on 40-man rosters will halt. Players and teams cannot communicate until a new CBA is agreed upon and ratified.

item.content:encoded:
Chicago Cubs outfielder Seiya Suzuki could be in line for a massive payday this offseason, with at least one team already generating buzz as a potential landing spot.
Jim Bowden of The Athletic ranks Suzuki as the No. 6 overall free agent in his latest rankings and projects the 32-year-old outfielder to land a five-year, $120 million contract, averaging $24 million per season.
Suzuki is coming off the best season of his MLB career, batting .270 with 26 home runs, 86 RBIs and a .368 on-base percentage. He also posted a .473 slugging percentage, an .841 OPS and a 131 OPS+ while producing 5.1 WAR, according to Baseball-Reference.
While Suzuki has always been a productive offensive player, his improved defense in right field helped make 2026 his most complete season since arriving from Japan.
Rumors are growing that the Toronto Blue Jays will make Suzuki a priority this offseason as they look to strengthen their outfield and add lineup protection for superstar Vladimir Guerrero Jr.
Bowden lists Toronto and the Philadelphia Phillies as the two best potential landing spots for Suzuki.
The veteran outfielder has been one of Chicago's most consistent hitters since signing his original five-year, $85 million contract ahead of the 2022 season. Over his five seasons with the Cubs, Suzuki averaged more than 20 home runs per year and posted an OPS+ of at least 125 in each of the past four seasons.
His combination of offensive consistency, improved defense and experience makes him one of the more attractive position players available in free agency.
Bowden compared Suzuki's potential contract to several notable outfield deals, including Teoscar Hernández's three-year, $66 million agreement, Jung Hoo Lee's six-year, $113 million contract and Nick Castellanos' five-year, $100 million deal.
For the Cubs, Suzuki's projected price tag presents another difficult offseason decision.
Chicago already faces significant uncertainty in its outfield, with several players potentially departing through free agency. Losing Suzuki would create another hole in a lineup that ranked among baseball's most productive offenses in 2026.
At $24 million annually, bringing Suzuki back would require a big financial commitment from the Cubs, who also need to address their starting rotation and several other roster needs.

item.title: [Bleacher Report] Brewers' Christian Yelich Sounds Off on World Series G4 Loss, 'Not Supposed to Be Easy'
item.dc:creator: Mike Chiari
item.description: Outfielder and team captain Christian Yelich summed things up following the Milwaukee Brewers' heartbreaking, 4-3 loss in extra innings to the Tampa Bay Rays in Game 4 of the World Series on Tuesday. Speaking to reporters after the Brewers allowed a golden opportunity to close out the series to slip through their fingers, Yelich said, "This stuff is not supposed to be easy. It's supposed to test you." Trailing by scores of 1-0 and 2-1, the Brewers twice battled back to tie things up in Game 4 th
item.content:encoded:
Outfielder and team captain Christian Yelich summed things up following the Milwaukee Brewers' heartbreaking, 4-3 loss in extra innings to the Tampa Bay Rays in Game 4 of the World Series on Tuesday.
Speaking to reporters after the Brewers allowed a golden opportunity to close out the series to slip through their fingers, Yelich said, "This stuff is not supposed to be easy. It's supposed to test you."
Trailing by scores of 1-0 and 2-1, the Brewers twice battled back to tie things up in Game 4 thanks to an RBI double by Cooper Pratt and solo home run by David Hamilton.
That allowed Milwaukee to force extra innings, and after the teams failed to score in the 10th and 11th innings, Pratt smacked a solo homer in the top of the 12th to put the Brewers ahead 3-2.
Milwaukee entered the bottom of the 12th needing three outs to win the first World Series in franchise history, but things went awry from there.
After Junior Caminero began the inning by reaching first base on a throwing error by Joey Ortiz, Shane Drohan entered the game and allowed four consecutive singles.
An RBI single by Jonny DeLuca tied it, and a walk-off RBI single by Ben Williamson won it, thus giving the Rays new life.
The Brewers still have a huge advantage, up 3-2 with likely National League Cy Young Award winner Jacob Misiorowski set to take the mound in Game 5 on Wednesday, but it is fair to wonder if losing Game 4 in such dramatic fashion could potentially mess with the Brew Crew's psyche.

item.content:encoded:
The MLB World Series is finally here after several weeks of intense playoff action. The Brewers swept the Dodgers to reach the World Series for the first time in 44 years. The Rays beat out the Guardians in six games to win the American League pennant for just the third time. Just like in this year's WNBA Finals, we're about to witness history: Whoever wins, this will be the franchise's first championship.
The Milwaukee Brewers are currently in the lead with three wins; they only need one more to win the entire World Series. But it's still anyone's game. Which team will come out on top? Here's how you can watch tonight's World Series game live, even for free.
What Time Is the Milwaukee Brewers vs. Tampa Bay Rays Game?
Game 5 of the World Series between the Rays and Brewers will take place on Wednesday, October 28, at 8:00 p.m. ET.
How to Watch the Milwaukee Brewers vs. Tampa Bay Rays?
This year, the World Series will be broadcast on Fox and the Fox One app. You can also watch it with a live TV or sports streaming subscription from DirecTV, Fubo, Hulu, Sling, Sportsnet+ (if you're in Canada), or YouTube TV.
How to Watch the Brewers vs. Rays for Free
If you don't want to subscribe to any of the above platforms, you may be able to sign up for a few free trials to gain access to the remaining games. Fox One and Hulu offer three-day trials, DirecTV and Fubo offer five days, and YouTube TV gives you 10 days for free.
2026 MLB World Series Game Schedule
MLB's expanded postseason means more teams on the playoff schedule. In the Wild Card round, the Braves beat the Phillies, the Padres beat the Cubs, the Yankees defeated the Red Sox, and the White Sox defeated the Astros. The winners advanced to the Division Series, where the Los Angeles Dodgers, Milwaukee Brewers, Tampa Bay Rays, and Cleveland Guardians beat their respective opponents.
For the Championship Series, the Brewers beat the Dodgers in four games to clinch the National League pennant. The Rays defeated the Guardians in six games to capture the American League pennant. Now, Milwaukee and Tampa Bay will face off in the best-of-seven World Series to begin on October 23. Who will get to raise the trophy?
World Series: Milwaukee Brewers vs. Tampa Bay Rays - MIL leads 3-1
- Game 5 on October 28 - Fox/Fox One*
- Game 6 on October 30 - Fox/Fox One*
- Game 7 on October 31 - Fox/Fox One*
*if necessary
How to Stream the 2026 MLB Playoffs
This year's MLB postseason is stretched across multiple networks and streaming services. All Wild Card Series games for the American League and National League were broadcast on NBC, NBCSN, and Peacock. ALDS and ALCS games were on TBS/TruTV and HBO Max, while NLDS and NLCS games were on Fox/FS1. For the World Series, all games will be broadcast on Fox and the Fox One streaming service.
- DirecTV: DirecTV's MySports base pack costs $45 per month for the first six months to see every game on Fox, FS1, NBC, and TBS/TruTV.
- Fox One: Fox's own streaming app lets you watch the NLDS, NLCS, and World Series on Fox and FS1 for $20 per month.
- Fubo: Fubo's Sports plan costs $45.99 for the first month to watch the Wild Card Series, NLDS, NLCS, and World Series on Fox, FS1, and NBC/NBCSN.
- HBO Max: If you pay for the $18.49-per-month HBO Max Standard, you'll be able to watch the ALDS and ALCS games on TBS/TruTV.
- Hulu: For $90 per month, you can watch every game on Fox, FS1, NBC, TBS, and TruTV.
- Peacock: Instead of a live TV service, you'd need to pay $10.99 per month for Peacock Premium to see the Wild Card Series games.
- Sling: The $60.99-per-month Sling Orange & Blue bundle will let you watch the ALDS and ALCS on TBS/TruTV and the NLDS and NLCS on FS1. Day Passes are also available for Sling Orange, allowing you to watch games on TBS for up to seven days.
- Sportsnet+ (Canada only): The $30-per-month Standard tier lets you watch every postseason game.
- YouTube TV: Though the standard plan for YouTube TV costs $83 per month, you can actually now pay for the cheaper $65 Sports package to see all games on Fox, FS1, NBC/NBCSN, and TBS/TruTV.
Can I Watch Postseason Games on MLB.TV?
Are you already an MLB.TV subscriber? You can watch the Division Series, Championship Series, and World Series games through MLB's own streaming service—but there's a catch. To watch on MLB.TV, you'll first need to authenticate through a participating pay TV provider. It's such a sticking point that it makes the entire question moot. If you already have a TV provider, then you wouldn't need to use a streaming service. If you don't already have an MLB.TV subscription, don't pay for one now.
How can I listen to the 2026 postseason?
You can also listen to the games via ESPN Radio.
Which Teams Are In the Playoffs?
Since MLB expanded its postseason picture in 2022, a total of 12 teams make the playoffs each year. That includes six teams per league, including the three division winners and three Wild Card teams.
- American League Division Winners: Tampa Bay Rays (1), Cleveland Guardians (2), Houston Astros (3)
- American League Wild Card: New York Yankees (4), Boston Red Sox (5), Chicago White Sox (6)
- National League Division Winners: Milwaukee Brewers (1), Los Angeles Dodgers (2), Atlanta Braves (3)
- National League Wild Card: Chicago Cubs (4), Philadelphia Phillies (5), San Diego Padres (6)
Upgrade Your Streaming Experience
If you decide to watch the MLB postseason, there's still time to get a big-screen television for viewing this beautiful game. Pro tip: Turn on your TV's motion-smoothing option for the best picture while watching sports. Just remember to turn it off before watching other TV shows and movies to avoid the awful "soap opera" effect.
About Our Expert
As PCMag's editor of how to content, I have to cover a wide variety of topics and also make our stories accessible to everyday users. Considering my history as a technical writer, copywriter, and all-around freelancer covering baseball, comics, and more at various outlets, I am used to making myself into an expert.
I believe tech corporations are bad, but you might as well know how to use technology in everyday life. Want more how to content delivered right to your inbox? Sign up for the tips and tricks newsletter that I curate three times a week.
My job as how-to guru means I use just about every gadget under the sun, so I can figure out how everything works. I work from a Lenovo ThinkPad running Windows 11, but also have a very large Dell Inspiron 17 3000 and Apple silicon MacBook. I have a Google Pixel 6a for personal use and use a Galaxy Z Flip 4 for additional Samsung-related testing. For iOS coverage, an iPhone 13 mini works like a charm, though it's already becoming a little long in the tooth.
My desktop situation includes a dual monitor setup with a modest Acer monitor. I also use a Logitech vertical mouse (who can use these ThinkPad trackpads) and a Havit keyboard (my first mechanical keyboard; I love it but my wife hates it!). I'm a recent convert from wired headphones; I have Anker Soundcore Liberty Air wireless earbuds for personal use and have taken to the Sennheiser HD 450BT headphones for work.
Whenever I have a second to myself, I'm probably gaming on my Nintendo Switch 2, Steam Deck, or Xbox Series S. I also still have a bunch of classic consoles lying around as well.

item.description: In perhaps a precursor to the American League Cy Young Award voting, Toronto Blue Jays pitcher Dylan Cease was not named as the Most Outstanding American League Pitcher of the Year, falling in the voting to Cam Schlittler of the New York Yankees. item.content:encoded:
In perhaps a precursor to the American League Cy Young Award voting, Toronto Blue Jays pitcher Dylan Cease was not named as the Most Outstanding American League Pitcher of the Year, falling in the voting to Cam Schlittler of the New York Yankees.
The awards are voted on by the MLB Players Association.
Regardless of result, it was a great first season in Toronto for Cease, who signed a seven-year, $210 million deal last offseason.
The right-hander made 29 starts around two short injured list stints, going 11-6 with a 2.40 ERA. The Blue Jays had the fewest runs scored and fewest home runs in baseball this season, so Cease and the pitching staff were forced to carry the offense. And Cease certainly did his part.
He struck out 239 batters in just 169.0 innings, marking his sixth straight season of 200 strikeouts or more. He also led the American League in hits/9, strikeouts/9, and home runs/9.
An eight-year veteran of the Chicago White Sox, San Diego Padres and Blue Jays, he's 76-64 in his career with a 3.67 ERA.
He made the All-Star Game for the first time this season, earning the start for the American League, which was managed by Jays' skipper John Schneider.
He ended the year on the IL with shoulder inflammation but is expected to be healthy for spring training.
As for Cam Schlittler
The 25-year-old Massachusetts native made his major league debut in 2025 and has taken the league by storm ever since. Armed with a fastball in the upper-90s, he went 14-6 with a minuscule 1.95 ERA this season, also striking out 239 batters. In 193.2 innings, he had a WHIP of just 0.92. He was a major reason why the Yankees won the American League East and advanced to the American League Division Series, where they were beaten by the Tampa Bay Rays.
Elsewhere for the Blue Jays...
The Milwaukee Brewers currently lead the Rays 3-1 in the World Series with Game 5 set to come on Wednesday night.
If the Rays win, the series will shift back to Milwaukee for Game 6 on Friday, but if the Rays lose, the season is over.
Once the season ends, the pending free agents for the Blue Jays will officially exit the 40-man roster. The Blue Jays will then have five days to get their 40-man roster in compliance and free agency will begin.
However, it's unclear how active free agency will be in November as a result of the looming MLB lockout.

item.title: [CubsHQ] Pete Crow-Armstrong sweeps two major MLB Players Choice Awards
item.dc:creator: Tony Crumpton
item.description: Chicago Cubs center fielder Pete Crow-Armstrong continues to add to his impressive awards after a historic 2026 season. The Major League Baseball Players Association announced Wednesday that Crow-Armstrong has won both the 2026 Players Choice Awards Player of the Year and National League Outstanding Player honors. Unlike awards voted on by baseball writers, the Players Choice Awards are determined exclusively by active MLB players, making the recognition even more meaningful for the 24-year-old
item.content:encoded:
Chicago Cubs center fielder Pete Crow-Armstrong continues to add to his impressive awards after a historic 2026 season.
The Major League Baseball Players Association announced Wednesday that Crow-Armstrong has won both the 2026 Players Choice Awards Player of the Year and National League Outstanding Player honors.
Unlike awards voted on by baseball writers, the Players Choice Awards are determined exclusively by active MLB players, making the recognition even more meaningful for the 24-year-old Cubs star.
Crow-Armstrong put together one of the greatest individual seasons in franchise history, batting .280 with 45 home runs, 107 RBIs, 119 runs scored and 41 stolen bases. He also posted a .372 on-base percentage, .570 slugging percentage and .942 OPS while appearing in all 162 games.
His 45 home runs tied Philadelphia Phillies slugger Kyle Schwarber for the major league lead, while his 41 stolen bases made him just the seventh player in MLB history to record at least 40 home runs and 40 stolen bases in the same season. He also became the first Cubs player to accomplish the feat.
What makes Crow-Armstrong's season even more remarkable is his ability to impact games on both sides of the ball.
According to the MLBPA, Crow-Armstrong became the first player since Hall of Famer Cal Ripken Jr. in 1991 to finish among FanGraphs' top three players in both offensive and defensive value.
His combination of power, speed and elite defense in center field helped establish him as one of baseball's most complete players.
Crow-Armstrong was selected over fellow Player of the Year finalists Shohei Ohtani and Yordan Alvarez. He also beat out Ohtani and Schwarber for the NL Outstanding Player honor.
The latest recognition adds to an already impressive offseason for Crow-Armstrong, who has also received Player of the Year honors from Baseball America and Baseball Digest.

item.title: [Field Level Media] Brewers turn to Jacob Misiorowski in 2nd attempt to end World Series

With the Rays down to their last three outs, Jonny DeLuca and Ben Williamson provided the heroics to alter the narrative after Tampa Bay had been stymied at every turn over the first three games by the Milwaukee Brewers. item.content:encoded:
ST. PETERSBURG, Fla. — With some pent-up energy and a fearless attitude, the Tampa Bay Rays extended their season at least one more day and will play host to Game 5 of the World Series on Wednesday.
With the Rays down to their last three outs, Jonny DeLuca and Ben Williamson provided the heroics to alter the narrative after Tampa Bay had been stymied at every turn over the first three games by the Milwaukee Brewers.
After falling into a 3-0 series hole, the Rays will now try to lean into their new-found momentum, but first they need to come up with a pitching plan.
Tampa Bay right-hander Nick Martinez would have been the probable Game 5 starter, but he was needed to pitch two innings on Tuesday.
“We’re going to get together after this session and sit down and talk about pitching,” Rays manager Kevin Cash said after the victory. “Going to check who’s available. I’m going to guess most guys are going to say they’re capable of an inning or more given it’s Game 5 of the World Series, but nothing has been decided yet.”
The Brewers tied the Tuesday game 2-2 in the fifth inning on a home run from David Hamilton, and the score remained even until the 12th when Cooper Pratt hit a home run for Milwaukee.
Down 3-2, Tampa Bay caught a rare break when Brewers third baseman Joey Ortiz committed a throwing error on Junior Caminero’s grounder to open the bottom of the 12th. Liam Hicks singled before DeLuca delivered an RBI single to center to tie the game 3-all.
After a Chandler Simpson single loaded the bases with no outs, Williamson came on to pinch-hit and bounced a ball into right field to set off a Rays celebration on the infield.
“Cash just kind of turned around and said, ‘Get ready to hit,'” Williamson said. “Jokingly in my head, I was thinking, ‘Yeah, I’ve been ready to hit since the fourth or fifth inning.'”
The Brewers now have one more opportunity to clinch their first-ever World Series title on the road, then would play host to Games 6 and 7, if necessary.
“Nobody said any of this was going to be easy, but I think we have the right group to get a good night’s sleep, flush it and be ready to go (Wednesday),” said Brewers first baseman Jake Bauers, who is 2-for-17 with three walks in the series after winning the National League Championship Series MVP award.
While Tampa Bay scrambles to put together a pitching plan, Milwaukee will send NL Cy Young Award favorite Jacob Misiorowski to the mound. The hard-throwing right-hander allowed one run over five innings to earn the win in Game 1.
In three starts and 13 1/3 innings this postseason, Misiorowski is 1-0 with a 2.70 ERA and 14 strikeouts, although he had just three against the Rays in the series opener.
“You can write it up and hope that they perform like the back of their baseball card, but that doesn’t always happen,” Brewers manager Pat Murphy said after announcing Misiorowski as his starter. “You go with what you believe is the deal. I trust our guys. They put themselves in a position to win.”
While the Rays used seven pitchers to keep their season alive in Game 4, the Brewers went even deeper by using eight in an unsuccessful attempt to close out their first-ever World Series championship. Game 5 could come down to which bullpen bounces back best.
“You’re seeing two elite contact offenses where strikeouts are very tough to come by,” Cash said. “We weren’t knocking balls in the gap or knocking balls out of the ballpark. We pieced together a big (12th inning), maybe the most important inning of our season.”
–Field Level Media

item.content:encoded:
The Toronto Blue Jays and Seiya Suzuki have been paired as a match for months.
It's easy enough during a given MLB season to look at upcoming free agents from multiple rosters and figure out who might have openings and who might have money to spend.
The Blue Jays have basically aligned with Suzuki, the free agent outfielder from the Chicago Cubs, in every way.
They'd even have a chance for him to join his Japanese countryman, Kazuma Okamoto, who just had a solid debut season in Toronto.
Free agency hasn't officially arrived yet, but that hasn't stopped the rumor mills and speculation from continuing.
And the latest update for the Blue Jays and Suzuki continues to suggest that they could end up together.
Seiya Suzuki Blue Jays Update
The Athletic's Jim Bowden wrote on Tuesday that he sees the Blue Jays as one of the best fits for Suzuki in free agency.
Bowden notes the Philadelphia Phillies as the team Toronto could have to compete with, and it's worth adding that Bowden has the Phillies interested in Randy Arozarena, too, but not the Blue Jays. So if Philadelphia ended up with Arozarena, that could help the Blue Jays get Suzuki.
"There is a lot of scuttlebutt in the industry that the Blue Jays are going to be targeting him as they look to add more offense to their outfield and more protection in their lineup for Vladimir Guerrero Jr.," writes Bowden. "Suzuki was a consistent performer for the Cubs over the past five years, averaging over 20 homers per season and an OPS+ of at least 125 over the past four seasons."
After a season in which the Blue Jays missed the playoffs, they certainly won't want to go the entire offseason without making a splash. Suzuki would qualify, particularly in a weak free agent hitter market.
Given all the chatter, there's really no surprise that Bowden is linking Suzuki to the Blue Jays, too. They'll still have to close the deal at some point.
Seiya Suzuki Contract Projection
Bowden also provided a contract projection for Suzuki as part of his blurb. He predicts a five-year deal for $120 million, which would be $24 million per year.
"Suzuki is coming off the best year of his MLB career," Bowden writes. "He had a .270/.368/.473 slash line with 26 homers and a 131 OPS+. He not only ranked among the better hitters in batting run value, but he improved his defense in right to become an asset there as well."
In a better free agent class, Suzuki might fly under the radar. In this one, he's going to be one of the prized signings, and the Blue Jays sure seem to be hoping he can be theirs.
This article was originally published on HEAVY
The post Blue Jays' Seiya Suzuki Update Says What Everyone Is Thinking appeared first on HEAVY.

Game 4 of the World Series between the Milwaukee Brewers and Tampa Bay Rays begins at 8:00 p.m. ET on Tuesday, October 27, televised by FOX. The Brewers are favored with a 1.75x payout to win on PrizePicks.
The Milwaukee Brewers lead 3-0 in the World Series after routing the Tampa Bay Rays 10-1 in Game 3 on Monday. Milwaukee is now one win away from securing the franchise's first World Series championship, while Tampa Bay faces elimination and must win four consecutive games to complete an improbable comeback.
The Rays will turn to SP Griffin Jax in Game 4, hoping the right-hander can slow down a Brewers lineup that has dominated the World Series. Milwaukee has not announced its starting pitcher, potentially setting up another bullpen game as the club looks to complete the sweep.
Below, we'll break down our Brewers vs. Rays prediction and picks for Tuesday's World Series Game 4, including the winner and player picks for PrizePicks.

Brewers vs. Rays Prediction, Winner Payout, Over/Under for World Series Game 4
Milwaukee enters Game 4 as the road favorite, returning a 1.75x payout if it wins outright.
Here are the full payouts for the Brewers vs. Rays game. PrizePicks data is live at the time of writing and is subject to change.

Griffin Jax (3.41 xFIP) will take the ball for Tampa Bay as the Rays' season hangs in the balance. The right-hander finished the regular season 8-10 with a 3.53 ERA and 116 strikeouts.
He faces a tough assignment against a Milwaukee offense that has consistently put runners on base throughout the World Series, but his regular-season home success could help him tonight.
Jax has struggled during the postseason, allowing 4 earned runs over six innings in his previous playoff appearances.
We can talk all we want about Tampa’s pitching plans, but ultimately the Rays offense will need a much better showing against Milwaukee's pitching staff if they want to save their season.
Despite being so good at getting runners on base and capitalizing with runners in scoring position during the regular season, the Rays managed just 1 run and struggled to generate sustained offense in Game 3. Those same issues plagued Tampa Bay in the first two games of this series.
The Brewers' pitching plans remain uncertain heading into tonight. Milwaukee has not announced a starter, and a bullpen-heavy approach seems most likely with the championship within reach.
The Brewers used LHP Robert Gasser in Game 3, and he delivered one of the postseason's most dominant starts, allowing just 1 hit over six innings while striking out 6.
Gasser's performance gave Milwaukee's bullpen valuable rest, which could prove significant if the Brewers need multiple relievers to get through Game 4. Milwaukee's pitching staff has been outstanding throughout the postseason, allowing just 7 runs across its first three World Series games.
The Brewers offense has stolen the show this World Series. At one point last night, they recorded eight straight two-out hits to blow the game wide open — a truly magnificent team feat on the grandest stage of all.

- The Rays went 58-27-0 at home this season; their 68.2% home win rate ranked second in baseball, behind the Brewers.
- Griffin Jax's regular-season home xFIP was 2.82, a full run better than his 4.08 road xFIP.
- The Brewers didn’t need to use any of their high-leverage arms last night, and neither did the Rays, who essentially conceded the game in the fifth inning. This leaves Tampa Bay’s best relievers ready to come in, and perhaps used slightly more aggressively than Milwaukee’s, given the lack of margin for error in an elimination game.
- While the Brewers’ pen has been awesome this postseason, their 3.57 xFIP sits well above a 1.34 ERA. Also, their .220 BABIP could signal regression in what is shaping up to be a bullpen game for the Brew Crew.

item.content:encoded:
Toronto Blue Jays catcher Alejandro Kirk attended Game 3 of the World Series on Monday night at Tropicana Field.
Kirk and his wife, Sofia Castañeda, went to cheer on his childhood best friend, Tampa Bay Rays first baseman Jonathan Aranda. Castañeda shared the moment on Instagram.
It was the second straight round in which Kirk watched Aranda in person. Aranda’s father also spoke about the two friends and their long road together.
Jonathan Aranda’s Dad Sends Touching Message About Alejandro Kirk
Humberto Aranda, Jonathan’s father, attended Game 3 as well. He spoke with Mexican media about his son and Kirk during the World Series.
“Definitely seeing Alejandro, seeing Jonathan, seeing them here after so many years of following them… they played together, they started playing together at the age of three and this path that they are still following together is completely rewarding,” he said. “And for the families, for both families, the journey has been very good, very beautiful, and we are very happy to be able to live the experience.”
Humberto was an assistant coach on the boys’ Little League team in Tijuana, Mexico. Kirk’s father, Juan Manuel Kirk, managed that team.
Kirk and Aranda have been friends since they were 3. They played on the same youth teams for 12 years. They still work out at the same gym in Tijuana.
The friends traded places this fall. Last October, Aranda watched from the stands as Kirk played in the World Series. He wore a jersey from their old Tijuana youth team, the Glu-Glu, with a World Series patch.
When Kirk homered in Game 1, Aranda started a social media campaign to recover the ball. “It was a big thing for me to go see him,” Aranda said during the ALCS.
Now Kirk is returning the favor.
Alejandro Kirk Also Watched Aranda Clinch the Pennant at Tropicana Field
Monday was not Kirk’s first trip to Tropicana Field this postseason. He attended Game 6 of the American League Championship Series on Oct. 19.
Kirk has been keeping up with games at Tropicana Field. He has been in the area for work. He has been training at the Blue Jays’ player development complex in Dunedin, Florida.
Kirk was spotted at the complex on Oct. 23, getting an early start on the 2027 season. The current collective bargaining agreement expires Dec. 1. A lockout after that date would bar players on 40-man rosters from team facilities.

item.title: [Blog Red Machine] Reds get laughable Randy Arozarena suggestion from someone who should know better
item.dc:creator: Drew Koch
item.description: Jim Bowden was the general manager of the Cincinnati Reds for almost 11 years. Nowadays, he moonlights as some sort of MLB insider, appearing on various podcasts while also writing for The Athletic. Bowden's latest column featured the top-40 MLB free agents with contract predictions and team fits. Hilariously, Bowden named the Reds as a "fit" for Randy Arozarena. Okay, Jim, we'll play along. item.content:encoded:
Jim Bowden was the general manager of the Cincinnati Reds for almost 11 years. Nowadays, he moonlights as some sort of MLB insider, appearing on various podcasts while also writing for The Athletic. Bowden's latest column featured the top-40 MLB free agents with contract predictions and team fits. Hilariously, Bowden named the Reds as a "fit" for Randy Arozarena.
Okay, Jim, we'll play along. Yes, the Reds would undoubtedly love to have Arozarena's bat in the middle of their lineup next season. Few free agent hitters offer the type of upside that Arozarena could bring. He hit .281/.381/.484 with 26 home runs, 79 RBI, 26 stolen bases, and a 148 OPS+ with the Seattle Mariners last season.
Arozarena is a three-time All-Star who's right-handed bat would be a perfect fit in the Reds' left-handed heavy outfield. His defense doesn't necessarily fit Terry Francona's emphasis on playing "clean baseball", but Tito would probably make an exception if it meant having another dynamic bat to match the hitting prowess of Elly De La Cruz and Sal Stewart in 2027.
You know, Jim, you might be onto something here. Arozarena would be a terrific fit for the Reds this offseason. How much would it take to sign him? Oh!
Randy Arozarena to the Reds falls apart the moment you see the price tag
You see, that's where Bowden's idea falls off a cliff. The contract prediction for Arozarena is five years at $124 million. That's a $24.8 million AAV, just south of what Joey Votto was making during his last few years in a Reds uniform.
The fact that Bowden even mentioned the Reds as a possible fit just reveals how invalid his opinion is. While he didn't work under the Castellini during his time with the Reds, he knows better than anybody that Cincinnati doesn't have the resources to pursue a player like Arozarena in free agency.
Yes, the Reds targeted Kyle Schwarber last winter, but as every fan throughout the tri-state knows, that was a one-off situation. Cincinnati was trying to lure the Middletown native back home and reportedly offered him a five-year, $125 million. Schwarber eventually re-signed with the Philadelphia Phillies, and the Reds never pivoted to another big bat like Pete Alonso, Alex Bregman, or Cody Bellinger.
Listing Arozarena as a "best fit" for the Reds is like suggesting a Rolls-Royce is the best fit for a line cook at a fast food restaurant. It's just not going to happen. Try again, Jimbo.

item.title: [Yahoo Sports] Three years ago, Corey Seager went deep
item.dc:creator: Adam J Morris
item.description: There are a few candidates for the greatest moment in Texas Rangers history. You could potentially including, I guess, Nolan Ryan's no hitters or Kenny Rogers' perfect game, but otherwise, pretty much all of them, I think, come in the 21st century, which says something about the first 30-something years of the team's history. There's Neftali Feliz fanning ARod to send the Rangers to their first every World Series in 2010. There's Cliff Lee striking out 13 Yankees in a two hit complete game shuto
item.content:encoded:
There are a few candidates for the greatest moment in Texas Rangers history. You could potentially including, I guess, Nolan Ryan's no hitters or Kenny Rogers' perfect game, but otherwise, pretty much all of them, I think, come in the 21st century, which says something about the first 30-something years of the team's history.
There's Neftali Feliz fanning ARod to send the Rangers to their first every World Series in 2010.
There's Cliff Lee striking out 13 Yankees in a two hit complete game shutout in Game 3 of the ALCS.
In 2011, Nelson Cruz's 11th inning walk off grand slam against the Tigers in the ALCS was magical.
As an Ian Kinsler stan, his 9th inning homer in Game 5 of the 2011 ALDS against the Rays, with him skipping out of the box on the way to first base, is still a favorite.
The five home runs Adolis Garcia hit in the 2023 ALCS against the Houston Astros — especially the Game 6 grand slam, after striking out his first four at bats, to blow the game open — tremendous.
But to me, the greatest moment in Texas Rangers history took place three years ago today. Game 1 of the 2023 World Series, in Arlington. The Rangers, down 5-3 going to the bottom of the ninth against D-Backs closer Paul Sewald. Leody Taveras leads off with a walk, bringing the tying run to the plate. Marcus Semien strikes out.
And then, up steps Corey Seager, and first pitch…
I don't know how many times I've watched that clip — dozens, at least. And it still gives me goosebumps.
"He could tie it with one swing…HIGH DRIVE…ITS TIED!!!"
I defy you to watch that clip and not have big feelings.
That was a $325 million dollar swing. That was the greatest moment in Texas Rangers history.
That home run just tied up the score, but at that moment I knew — much like I knew, when Mitch Garver homered in the second inning of Game 6 of the ALCS in Houston to tie up the game, that the Rangers would win the ALCS — that the Rangers were going to win, not just the game, but the whole damn thing.
Two innings later, Adolis Garcia won the game for the Rangers in dramatic fashion:
You know, we know, intellectually, that Adolis Garcia was a beast in the 2023 playoffs. We remember that he came up huge. But watching that clip, and the one of the ALCS homers, brings the feeling back.
Five days later, in Arizona, in a game where the Rangers didn't have a baserunner until the fifth inning, and didn't get a hit until the seventh, a gritty performance by Nathan Eovaldi kept the D-Backs off the scoreboard for six innings. Aroldis Chapman retired a pair of batters and issued a walk in the seventh before turning the ball over to Josh Sborz, who recorded the final seven outs.
And in an echo of 2010 and Neftali Feliz, Sborz ended the game with a backwards K:
For as long as I can remember, I've been a Rangers fan. As a kid, I was desperate to see the Rangers win the World Series, to be crowned champions. As an adult — especially after 2011 and 2012 — I started to think it would never happen, that the Rangers were cursed, and that I'd never see them lift the trophy.
Sometimes I find myself wondering, why do I do this to myself? Why am I a fan of this team? Why do I subject myself to the heartache and heartbreak and disappointment that is such a regular part of our fandom?
And then I watch those clips above, and my question is answered. 2023 makes it all worthwhile.

item.title: [roundtable.io] Boston Red Sox Free Agency: Could Red Sox Enter Bidding War for Top Japanese Slugger?
item.dc:creator: Zach Coe
item.description: One insider projects a big-market bidding war for free-agent slugger Teruaki Sato. With the Milwaukee Brewers holding a commanding 3-0 series lead over the Tampa Bay Rays in the World Series, the offseason is officially on the doorstep. As the Boston Red Sox put the finishing touches on their offseason plan, one insider, former Cincinnati Reds and Washington Nationals GM and The Athletic writer Jim Bowden, projects a “big market bidding war,” including Boston, for top international free agent, t
item.content:encoded:
One insider projects a big-market bidding war for free-agent slugger Teruaki Sato.
With the Milwaukee Brewers holding a commanding 3-0 series lead over the Tampa Bay Rays in the World Series, the offseason is officially on the doorstep. As the Boston Red Sox put the finishing touches on their offseason plan, one insider, former Cincinnati Reds and Washington Nationals GM and The Athletic writer Jim Bowden, projects a “big market bidding war,” including Boston, for top international free agent, third baseman Teruaki Sato.
About Sato
The 27-year-old spent most of 2026 at third base with the Hanshin Tigers in NPB. In 143 games, Sato hit .306/.383/.609/.991, led the league with 40 doubles, 39 home runs, and 106 runs driven in. Sato has some concerns, though: he struck out at a 26.7 percent rate in 2026, the third-highest in NPB. However, an 11.1 percent walk rate offset that somewhat; it was the ninth-highest in the league.
Defensively, Sato profiles as a below-average third baseman. He also spent time in right field in 2026, where he was also below average. Ultimately, the 27-year-old could find a long-term home at first base or as a designated hitter.
Hanshin posted Sato on Oct. 19; he has 45 days to sign with a team. However, that clock will pause at the start of the lockout on Dec. 1 at 11:59 p.m. ET if he is not signed by then.
What did Bowden say?
“Some teams believe he can stay at third base; others see him as best suited for first base or left field. Either way, the bat profiles for the middle of the order. I think he stays at third base initially and would be a perfect fit for teams like the Phillies, Red Sox, Angels and Yankees, which leads me to believe this will end up being a big-market bidding war,” Bowden wrote on Tuesday.
Will the Red Sox spend that much on Sato?
Put me in the camp that is skeptical that Sato will land a deal that pays him $36 million annually, even if a bidding war emerges among the big-market teams Bowden lists as potential suitors. It is worth noting that both Chicago White Sox first baseman Munetaka Murakami and Toronto Blue Jays third baseman Kazuma Okamoto were projected to land much higher deals than the ones they eventually signed (two-year, $34-million for Murakami and four-year, $60 for Okamoto).
Murakami faced concerns similar to Sato's about his strikeout rate and how it would translate to Major League Baseball. While Murakami struck out 35.4 percent of the time, the second-highest rate in baseball, he also hit 35 home runs, posted a .478 slugging percentage, and walked 16.6 percent of plate appearances. Murakami’s success in Chicago will surely help Sato’s market, but not by $19 million more annually.
While Bowden projects Sato will stay at third base, Boston already has the likely Gold Glove Award winner at the position in Caleb Durbin. They’ll want to stick with him at the hot corner after building so much of their team identity on pitching and defense. With All-Star Willson Contreras handling first base, Sato would likely be a designated hitter in Boston at least for the remainder of Contreras’ contract, which has a team option for 2028.
Now, financially, the Red Sox are in a precarious spot. With $268 million committed to 2027 before any additions, the team projects to be over the second-luxury tax threshold for what would be the third straight season. With so much of the financial landscape in flux due to the ongoing labor negotiations, it seems unlikely the team will add significant money before the lockout without first moving some money off the books. That said, if Sato’s market is closer to the $25-million AAV Spotrac projects, the 27-year-old seems like an ideal target for Boston.

This could be the final MLB game for quite some time as the Milwaukee Brewers have a chance to sweep the Tampa Bay Rays in the 2026 World Series on Tuesday night.
Milwaukee scored eight runs with two outs in the fifth inning in Game 3 last night, putting up 10 runs without a home run in the 10-1 victory.
There have now been just two home runs through three games in this series, both of which came in Game 2.
Nevertheless, I have a home run pick for each team in World Series Game 4 tonight.
Here’s a complete breakdown of these home run props for Tuesday, Oct. 27.
Best MLB Home Run Prop Bet Picks for Tuesday, Oct. 27.
- Yandy Diaz to Hit a Home Run (+800)
- William Contreras to Hit a Home Run (+540)
Yandy Diaz to Hit a Home Run (+800)
There weren’t any home runs in Game 3, but Yandy Diaz came pretty darn close. His 413-foot double with an exit velocity of 111.4 miles per hour would’ve been a home run in 22 of 30 ballparks, according to Baseball Savant. He also had a single with an exit velocity of 115.5 miles per hour.
Diaz had 22 home runs in the regular season and went deep twice in the ALCS. I’ll take this long +800 price given the power he has and how well he’s seeing the ball right now.
William Contreras to Hit a Home Run (+540)
I am going down with the ship.
After hitting 18 home runs in the regular season, Contreras has gone deep three times this postseason. The last one came in NLCS Game 2, the start of a six-game hitting streak for the slugger.
Contreras is now 18-for-43 (.419) with three home runs and a double in 11 postseason games. He’s racked up eight RBI and six runs as well.

item.title: [North Side Baseball] How Alex Bregman's Arrival Brought Dansby Swanson Back to the Shortstop Upper Crust—For Now
item.dc:creator: Matthew Trueblood
item.description: Cubs Video What Alex Bregman can do on the field—the statistical contribution he can make when it's his turn to bat and when the ball is hit his way—is plenty valuable. By the end of the 2026 season, that was obvious. Bregman was one of the best hitters in baseball from mid-July onward, and he won the Fielding Bible Award at third base for his supernal defense. Multiple teams were willing to give him a fat five-year deal last offseason, and most of that money is for the way he hits and fields. H
item.content:encoded:
Cubs Video
What Alex Bregman can do on the field—the statistical contribution he can make when it's his turn to bat and when the ball is hit his way—is plenty valuable. By the end of the 2026 season, that was obvious. Bregman was one of the best hitters in baseball from mid-July onward, and he won the Fielding Bible Award at third base for his supernal defense. Multiple teams were willing to give him a fat five-year deal last offseason, and most of that money is for the way he hits and fields.
However, Bregman also has enormous value as a facilitator, a leader, and an organization changer. That's what made the Cubs willing to outbid the Red Sox and others for his services; it was the extra cushion they needed to feel safe spashing so much money on a player who would turn 32 just days after playing his first regular-season game for them. In those areas, he was arguably an even greater success in 2026 than on the stat sheet. The partnership of Bregman and Pete Crow-Armstrong, offensively, was about more than the fact that they hit back-to-back at the top of the lineup 24 times. They made improvements that followed the same patterns. They communicated about what they were seeing from each opposing pitcher. Bregman thrived down the stretch, but his input also helped Crow-Armstrong break the game, even while the veteran was still mired in a long early funk.
Defensively, his partnership would be with shortstop Dansby Swanson. Bregman replaced Swanson as the highest-paid player on the team and as the team's resident emblem of intention to win and dedication to whatever that takes. Swanson was the first overall pick in 2015; Bregman was the second. Swanson won the 2021 World Series with the team from near Atlanta. Bregman won the World Baseball Classic and the Series in 2017, then another Series in 2022. Swanson's championship came at Bregman's expense, too, as his club beat Houston in that Fall Classic. The two players' history was interwoven, and they would need to prove they could achieve as much together as they had (seemingly) working at odds, to top one another.
It couldn't have worked out more beautifully, or in a fashion more quintessentially Bregman. Here's the gist: In 2025, Swanson's defensive numbers dipped. That wasn't surprising. He was 31 years old, which is already getting a bit old for a shortstop in the majors today. He doesn't have an elite arm (or even, in truth, an average one), and though he learned long ago to get rid of the ball exceptionally quickly when needed, that can't make up for everything. He suffered, in particular, on exactly the balls you would expect an aging non-premium athlete to suffer on: ones hit to his right, where he had to range into the hole and make the toughest plays asked of shortstops. According to Baseball Savant, Swanson dropped from 16 and 12 runs saved in 2023 and 2024, respectively, to just 2 in 2025. The biggest difference came on balls that forced him to move toward third base:
- 2023: 8 Outs Above Average
- 2024: 2
- 2025: -1
The Cubs didn't do what many teams might have done in such a situation, though. First of all, they didn't even briefly consider moving Swanson to second base and trading Nico Hoerner. That would have been a viable option; Hoerner was an impending free agent until he signed a six-year extension last spring. The Cubs believed Swanson could still be a great defensive shortstop, though, and that Hoerner's defensive work as his double-play partner was too valuable to lose.
Even with the same personnel in place, though, they could have more aggressively shaded their infield alignments, putting Swanson a step or two closer to the hole when there was a chance he would be called upon to make a play there. Instead, they used fairly traditional setups. The 2025 Cubs were 17th in shading their infield, doing so 53% of the time against left-handed batters and 6% of the time against righties. That led to a lot of plays that looked like this.
Seeing the ball zip past Swanson like that makes him seem slow, but that's unfair. Alec Bohm hit that grounder at 104 miles per hour. To make the play, Swanson needed to be a step farther in the direction he had to go. Failing that, not even a younger, more explosive player would get there. But the even more telling plays, perhaps, were those that looked more like this.
This ball isn't hit so hard, and Swanson has the quick feet to run it down. However, because he started at a neutral position, he had to run an extra step or two before snaring the bounce. That meant throwing off-balance, on the run, which robbed him of the ability to be accurate and powerful. This is where being 31 and a bit less strong-armed than most shortstops caught up to him, but much of the reason was his starting position.
Early in 2026, the same thing was happening too often. Swanson would flag down a ball that seemed ticketed for left field, but because he did so at the very edge of his range, he still couldn't record an out.
Over time, though, a (literal) shift took place. Bregman, who played with one of the game's most aggressive shifting teams in Houston before the league outlawed the true shift, advocated for a bit more proactive shading with his new club. They didn't become an extreme team, but they did become one of the league leaders in that area. In 2026, the Cubs shaded their infield 67% of the time against lefties and 14% of the time against righties, moving them into the top seven in shading, overall. Swanson started making plays that he couldn't make the previous year.
There were balls, like the one above, that would have been clean singles to left field in 2025 but became great plays in 2026. There were also plenty that might have become infield hits in 2025, but which ended up looking routine this year.
Swanson's numbers rebounded, especially on those balls that took him toward third base: he got back to 8 OAA on them. The way OAA tabulates value, that actually took a bite out of Bregman. He rated worse (-6 OAA) on balls to his left than he ever has before. But Bregman didn't care. By playing closer to the line against right-handed batters, he was better able to set himself for long throws when he made a play along the foul line, and he got better coming in on slowly hit balls. He was the best he's ever been at third, precisely because he ceded a bit of range to his superb partner on the left side of the infield.
Communication between those two players is more important than many who watch the game from home might realize. They don't call each other off in quite the same way outfielders do, but there has to be an understanding between the shortstop and the third baseman: when to take a ball and when to let it go; whether your partner will break to cover a base, and how to back them up if they go for the ball instead; where your teammate should throw the ball, if fielding it took him in a direction that makes it hard for him to see the whole diamond. Bregman and Swanson worked gloriously together in their first year as a tandem, which helped the Cubs reach the postseason and provided hope for the short-term aging profile of each.
That doesn't mean it won't get harder. As each moves into his mid-30s, they'll have to continue communicating, adapting and adjusting. Working together is important, but it can't entirely make up for the fact that each individual is getting a bit older, a bit slower and a bit less able to react in the blink of an eye. Next year, the Cubs' infield defense will probably be worse. That's the nature of investing so much in players who would ordinarily move off their positions, and slotting them into a roster that doesn't permit them to do so. What we saw in the first year of Bregman and Swanson, though, is that they're likely to weather those degradations better than most, because of their savvy and their shared commitment to doing whatever it takes to win.

item.title: [Yahoo Sports] World Series 2026: Brewers' DH Christian Yelich turns pivotal play of World Series Game 3 with speed and instincts — 'Nobody cares about baserunning more than him'
item.dc:creator: Jake Mintz
item.description: ST. PETERSBURG — The Brewers won by a mile because they're obsessed with the inches. Nobody would describe the final outcome of Milwaukee's emphatic beatdown on Monday — a 10-1 drubbing of the Tampa Bay Rays in Game 3 of the World Series — as "close."
