item.content:encoded:
ST. PETERSBURG — The Brewers won by a mile because they're obsessed with the inches.
Nobody would describe the final outcome of Milwaukee's emphatic beatdown on Monday — a 10-1 drubbing of the Tampa Bay Rays in Game 3 of the World Series — as "close." Not since 2015 has there been a larger margin of victory in a World Series game. The Brewers' 16-to-3 hit advantage over the flailing Rays was the third-largest in Fall Classic history. Starter Robert Gasser allowed just one one hit and faced the minimum across six brilliant innings, becoming the first lefty to do that in a World Series game since Sandy Koufax in 1965. A massive gathering of Brewers fans, an estimated 30% of the crowd, was there to witness it all, their voices joyously hoarse by the end.
It was a shellacking of historic proportions.
But Milwaukee's commanding 3-0 series lead, one that places this franchise on the precipice of its first championship, was earned in the margins on a bang-bang play that folks in the Badger State will remember for a long time.
Up a pair in the top of the fifth, the Brewers put runners on first and second against Tampa Bay starter Freddy Peralta. Milwaukee catcher William Contreras, the best hitter in these playoffs, ripped a two-hopper toward third baseman Junior Caminero. In a spinning motion, Tampa's talented talisman snagged the pearl and flicked it to second baseman Ben Williamson as a full-bore Christian Yelich slid into the bag. Umpire Dan Bellino punched his fist. The FOX graphic evaporated from the screen. Multiple members of Tampa Bay's between-innings hype squad jogged onto the outfield track for some type of giveaway.
Yelich, though, clung to the bag with his left hand as he motioned adamantly toward Belino with his right.
"Safe, safe."
Safe, indeed.
The Brewers challenged the call. Before Bellino could finish announcing the overturn, Tampa Bay skipper Kevin Cash was already headed toward the mound to pull Peralta.
But no move, at that point, could have stopped the inevitable.
"The whole game was changed when Yeli was safe at second," Brewer manager Pat Murphy insisted afterwards. "That's just a hustle play. When your leader makes that play, that says it all. The game was changed because he did a little thing that anybody can do."
Yelich, by beating the throw to second, turned a dead frame into the inning of a lifetime. The floodgates soon burst, sweeping away Tampa's next pitcher, Cam Booser. On a 2-2 count, he served a mid-zone fastball to second baseman Brice Turang, who scorched one off shortstop Taylor Walls' glove and into the outfield. Milwaukee's lead was doubled.
As the sizable traveling contingent — a bar down the street sold out of Miller Lite before first pitch — went berzerk, the Fox broadcast panned to a young Rays fan, who could be seen uttering to his companion a harsh and humbling realization: "That's the series."
Milwaukee, though, would leave no doubt. And then some.
Their next five batters all found grass, with each consequential hit eliciting louder and louder roars from the armada of traveling Wisconsinites. In total, the Brewers strung together seven consecutive two-out hits to plate eight two-out runs, a World Series record. It was an all-time heater and a fitting performance from a pridefully selfless Brewers offense that has prioritized passing the baton over hitting big flies all season long.
"Nobody wants to be the hero," hitting coach Dan Vogelbach boasted.
That might be true, but Yelich, with his mad dash to second, was the under-the-radar hero of this evening.
With the right-handed Contreras at the plate and a runner on second, Rays first baseman Ryan Villade was shaded toward second, opting not to hold Yelich on. That allowed the Brewers' captain to take a much larger-than-average lead off first base. By the time Contreras swung, Yelich was already about 30 feet from the bag, his right foot in the air ready to break in either direction. As the ball bounced toward Caminero, Yelich landed and broke hard for second.
"You have to understand where you're at in space," Yelich explained postgame. "You're lengthening your primary [lead] in case there's a ball in the hole or some sort of play happens where you could potentially beat the throw."
It was a sublime bit of baserunning, the kind that takes years of purposeful, monotonous practice to get good at. There's also an element of internal pre-pitch preparation: "If X happens, I do Y." Yelich executed that process perfectly. Caminero, who had ample time to get the slow-footed Contreras at first, did not.
"The beauty of it is that you have guys like Yeli that demand it from the group," first-base coach Spencer Allen told Yahoo Sports about the team's attention to detail.
Jason Lane, Milwaukee's offense and strategy coordinator, explained to Yahoo Sports that he tells players to approach a secondary lead at first base and two outs with the same intent and intensity they would bring to a "contact play." That's the inside-baseball term for when a runner at third, with the infield drawn in, plans to race home on contact — no matter where the ball's hit.
"When you remind guys of that and explain it to them like that — and these guys are hunting all those little things that we preach about right turns — it can become something that happens in a playoff game," he explained.
On a team that cares deeply about the little things, Yelich, the group's most accomplished character, might care most of all. That establishes a standard, one that has helped push the Brewers to an amazing 10-1 record this postseason. But that crucial play, and its outcome, was about more than Yelich's impressive read and instincts. His footspeed from first to second clocked in at 28.5 mph, a full tick faster than his season average. That's an 81st-percentile result from a 34-year-old DH with a history of back problems.
Yelich was once a speedster before age and injuries did their thing. There exists a timeline in which the 2018 MVP evolved into a bat-first baseclogger, a plodder focused on in-box responsibilities. Instead, Yelich has done everything in his power to remain as athletic, as lithe and as quick as possible. Years of treatment, offseason sprint work, healthy habits, weight room sessions — all of it has allowed Yelich to maintain his speed despite the barrage of injuries and his status as a primary DH.
"I've got some things that have happened to me, but for the most part, I feel pretty good," he said when asked about his speed. "I feel like I can still hang with the boys out there."
The boys agree.
"That baserunning by Yeli there, which allowed us to have that huge inning ..." outfielder Sal Frelick said. "We work on those things in spring. He's the guy that's running the meeting, saying this is important. It's his 14th season. He's been All-Star, Silver Slugger, MVP, and nobody cares about baserunning more than him. Just to see him do that, get a good secondary, run as hard as he could and beat that out — that's what allowed us to have that big inning."
"Little things like that — that's what makes our team great."
Great might be an understatement. If the Brewers finish the deal in Game 4, they would become the first team in the League Championship Series era to sweep both the championship series and World Series rounds. They would finish this month a mind-boggling 11-1, with their only defeat coming by one run in NLDS Game 3 in San Diego. There's a strong argument that we are currently witnessing the most dominant postseason team in MLB history.
The gap between these Brewers and the rest of the league is a massive chasm, yes, but it's one they chiseled one swing and one step at a time.

item.content:encoded:
Después de 4 años de espera, México volverá a tener, por lo menos, un campeón de la Serie Mundial en 2026, pues independientemente de que los Milwaukee Brewers logren alzarse o sea el turno de triunfar de los Tampa Bay Rays, Joey Ortiz, JoJo Romero y Jonathan Aranda representarán la bandera tricolor en el máximo de los honores de la Major League Baseball (MLB).
En el caso particular de Aranda, el oriundo de Tijuana, Baja California ha tenido que remar contra corriente en más de una ocasión para poderse posicionar como uno de los mejores jugadores en la novena de Florida.
Jonathan Aranda ha sido un ejemplo de superación y de cómo no abandonar los sueños, pues a pesar de contar con el talento suficiente para poder llamar la atención de los scouts de la MLB, pasar casi una década en categorías menores, no poder encontrar una posición favorable y tener que superar lesión tras lesión ha forjado uno de los mejores peloteros mexicanos en la actualidad.
La visoria por Randy Arozarena
Curiosamente, el comienzo de la trayectoria profesional de Aranda está ligada con la de otro de los grandes referentes mexicanos en la MLB: Randy Arozarena. Tal como lo compartió Adam Berry para el propio sitio de la liga, el boricua Carlos Rodríguez, director de scouts internacionales de los Rays, viajó a Tijuana para visorear a un jardinero cubano (en ese entonces), que entrenaba precisamente en México, Randy Arozarena.
En aquel entonces, Tampa Bay no contaba con el presupuesto internacional suficiente para poder firmar a Randy Arozarena; sin embargo, esto no impidió que lograra encontrar un diamante en bruto. Arozarena nunca apareció en aquel entrenamiento, mientras que Rodríguez solicitó ver a los elementos más jóvenes de la academia de los Toros de Tijuana.
Rodríguez y los Rays quedaron impresionados con un joven Jonathan Aranda de 17 años y en ese entonces le ofrecieron 130 mil dólares para hacerse con sus servicios. El 2 de julio de 2015, el tijuanense firmó con Tampa Bay y a partir de ahí pasó por un total de 8 equipos dentro del sistema de categorías menores y mayores de la franquicia.
FIRST HOME RUN BELONGS TO JONATHAN ARANDA#ForTampaBay | #Postseason pic.twitter.com/WeB6rT8b8o
— Tampa Bay Rays (@RaysBaseball) October 3, 2026
Encontrar la posición indicada
Más allá del innegable talento de Jonathan Aranda, una de las cuestiones más grandes con el tijuanense era en qué posición se acoplaría mejor dentro del diamante, pues comenzó como segunda base y a lo largo de una década pasó por diversas posiciones dentro del cuadro. Incluso, tras la cancelación de la Temporada 2020 de Ligas Menores, intentaron probarlo como receptor o catcher.
Para 2021, Aranda respondió a los cuestionamientos de los críticos con un poderoso bateo en el equipo Doble A en Montgomery registrando una línea de .330/.418/.543, además de aportar 14 home runs y 22 dobles en 104 partidos. Por su parte, a lo largo de 3 temporadas entre 2022 y 2024, el mexicano controló el pitcheo de Triple A con un promedio de bateo de .315 y .959 de OPS.
No obstante, aún no lograba establecerse como titular con los Tampa Bay Rays debido a la escasez de oportunidades y la irregularidad con los tiempos de juego. Promediando .222 y un OPS de .692 en esos mismos 3 años pero en MLB. Esto además de tener como uno de sus principales enfoques el apuntalar su defensiva desde la primera base.
Team Mexico's Jonathan Aranda gets enough for a go-ahead three-run homer! #WorldBaseballClassic pic.twitter.com/gS78O7YaSy
— World Baseball Classic (@WBCBaseball) March 6, 2026
Un referente de los Rays
Para 2024, Aranda logró ganarse la oportunidad de ser el primera base titular de los Rays; sin embargo, una fractura en el dedo anular de la mano derecha, sufrida en el Spring Training, lo dejó fuera durante casi 2 meses. Historia similar a la que sucedió en 2025 cuando una colisión con Giancarlo Stanton (New York Yankees) le provocó una fractura en la muñeca izquierda.
Eso sí, durante la campaña 2025, Aranda se ganó el reconocimiento de ser llamado al Juego de Estrellas en Atlanta al tener .316 de promedio de bateo, .883 de OPS, además de aportar 14 vuelacercas y 59 carreras impulsadas. Al recuperarse de dicha lesión bateó home runs en juegos consecutivos.
Para la campaña 2026, Jonathan Aranda ha logrado consolidar un poderoso tridente en los Rays junto al cubano Yandy Díaz y al dominicano Junior Caminero, consolidando un orden de bateo temible para cualquier bullpen de la Major League Baseball.
En la actual temporada, Aranda tuvo un promedio de bateo de .274, OPS de .792, aportando 22 home runs, 92 carreras impulsadas y siendo un pelotero determinante para alcanzar la Serie Mundial ante los Milwaukee Brewers.

item.content:encoded:
Pete Fatse was fired alongside Alex Cora and five other members of the Red Sox coaching staff. Now, he has found a new home.
Former Boston Red Sox manager Alex Cora has dominated the day after making his first comments about his dismissal on the 'Baseball Isn't Boring' Podcast on Monday morning. However, one of his former staffers, hitting coach Peter Fatse, who was fired alongside Cora and five other members of the major league coaching staff on April 25, has reportedly found his next job.
Despite the obvious connection between Philadelphia and Boston through former Red Sox and now Phillies President of Baseball Operations Dave Dombrowski, the two did not cross paths in Boston. Fatse joined the team as an assistant hitting coach after Dombrowski was fired. However, Cora and Dombrowski still have a strong relationship, so it wouldn't come as a shock to find out that the former Red Sox manager put in a good word for Fatse with Dombrowski.
After joining the Red Sox staff in 2019, Fatse served as an assistant under former hitting coach Tim Hyers. After Hyers departed the Red Sox for the same role with the Texas Rangers after the 2021 season, Fatse was promoted to take his place.
In four seasons and one month under Fatse's tutelage, the Red Sox offense ranked in the top 10 in baseball in runs scored (3,156, 7th), batting average (.255, 6th), on-base percentage (.321, T-10th), slugging percentage (.417, 6th), and OPS (.738, 6th). However, the team under Fatse did strike out at a high clip, posting a 23.2 percent strikeout rate, tied for the 10th-highest in baseball.
After being fired alongside Cora, bench coach Ramon Vasquez, third-base coach Kyle Hudson, assistant hitting coaches Dillon Lawson and Joe Cronin, and game-planning coordinator Jason Varitek, Fatse joined the Tampa Bay Rays' research and development team as a hitting consultant over the summer.
He'll now take over a star-studded Phillies lineup featuring Bryce Harper, Kyle Schwarber, and Trea Turner after Philadelphia's second straight disappointing season, losing in the Wild Card round to the Atlanta Braves.
Where are the other former Red Sox coaches?
Fatse became the second former member of the Red Sox coaching staff to land a new job as a hitting coach this offseason, joining his former assistant Dillon Lawson, who was named the Marlins' hitting coach on Oct. 12.
As for Cora, after turning down an offer from Dombrowski to join him in Philadelphia as Phillies manager just days after his dismissal in Boston, he once again spurned his former boss in Boston, rejecting an offer to replace then-interim manager Mattingly in Philadelphia. However, Cora didn't completely rule out a return to the dugout in Monday's interview with WEEI's Rob Bradford.
Vasquez, Cora's top lieutenant in Boston, could emerge as a candidate for other managerial openings after being considered for jobs in years past. However, if nothing materializes on that front, he seems like a safe bet to join Cora if he returns to the dugout.
Finally, there's Varitek, a two-time World Series Champion and Red Sox Hall of Famer. Shortly after the firings, the team called Varitek's dismissal a "reassignment" to a different role in the organization, to be announced later. Earlier in the season, Kennedy was asked about Varitek's role on the team, saying Varitek was taking time away from baseball after being hit hard by the decision.
Kennedy was asked about Varitek's status within the organization in the annual end-of-season press conference on Oct. 5, telling reporters that the longtime catcher has not yet rejoined the organization in any capacity, but the two sides have "connected" with each other.
While the other coaches' finding new positions is certainly noteworthy, all eyes will remain on Cora and whether he will return to manage, whether in 2027 or later.

item.content:encoded:
The Tampa Bay Rays are favored to take Game 3 on Monday, but their chances of capturing their first ever World Series title have dwindled.
The Rays jumped out to a 4-0 first inning lead in Game 2, but through the game’s final eight innings the offense sputtered and the defense, nor pitching from ace Drew Rasmussen, was as sharp as needed to hold down the Brewers, who earned a 5-4 victory.
The pair of one-run victories in Milwaukee have put the Brewers in prime position for their first title. Nearly 81% of MLB teams that have generated a 2-0 series lead in the World Series have gone on to win the title.
To disrupt that statistic, the Rays will need to find a way to win Game 3. Kalshi traders make their odds 53% as of Monday morning.
For informational purposes only. Not trading advice. See full disclaimer below. Kalshi is the Official Prediction Market Partner of the Atlanta Braves, Los Angeles Dodgers, San Francisco Giants, San Diego Padres, and Boston Red Sox.
World Series Game 3 Odds: Rays favored in home ballpark
Right-handed pitcher Freddy Peralta had a rough start to his 2026 campaign when pitching for the New York Mets. But after being dealt to the Rays, he’s unlocked a former version of himself, one the Milwaukee Brewers know quite well. Peralta pitched for the Brewers for eight seasons before being traded to the Mets in the offseason. The Mets dealt him to the Rays at the trade deadline.
As such, now he’ll need to square off against his former team in World Series Game 3, looking to extend an incredible stretch of pitching which saw him earn ALCS MVP honors.
Across three starts and one relief appearance this postseason, Peralta has thrown 16.2 innings and allowed just two earned runs, good for a 1.08 ERA.
But the Brewers represent a level up offensively. Milwaukee finished the regular season tied for first in wRC+ against right-handed starters and led the league in on-base percentage and batting average against the handedness.
On the other hand, the Rays will draw left-handed starter Robert Gasser. Like the rest of the Milwaukee staff, Gasser has been fantastic this postseason, throwing nine innings over the course of two starts and allowing just one earned run.
Southpaws have been a challenge for the Rays this season, with the team ranking 26th against lefties in terms of wRC+ during the regular season. Even if they are able to get through Gasser, the Milwaukee bullpen features lefties JoJo Romero, DL Hall, and Aaron Ashby, and has been nearly unhittable, collectively posting a 1.23 ERA in nearly 51 innings this postseason.
Nevertheless, Kalshi traders make the Rays, who posted a 55-26 record at home during the regular season, slight favorites at 53% in Game 3.
The Rays overcame a 2-1 deficit in the ALCS, but they face a stiffer test against baseball’s top team in the World Series.
Regardless of the Game 3 winner, Game 4 will take place on Tuesday in Tampa Bay. In early trading, Kalshi traders make the Brewers slight favorites on the road in that game, pricing them at 50%.
Should a Game 5 be necessary, it will take place on Wednesday in Tampa Bay. If Games 6 or 7 are required, those will take place back in Milwaukee after a travel day.
Through two games, Brewers catcher William Contreras is the favorite for World Series MVP, according to Kalshi traders.
Contreras is trading around 38% to earn the award while outfielder Jackson Chourio is trading at 17% and left-handed reliever Aaron Ashby is priced at 15%.
In their two home victories, Contreras has notched four hits in eight at-bats and driven in two runs for Milwaukee. Plus, he’s thrown out multiple runners attempting to steal and helped manage a pitching staff through two tense one-run victories.
Chourio has posted similar stats, netting four hits in his nine at-bats, while stealing two bases and cutting down a runner at the plate with an outfield assist during Game 2.
Though less heralded coming into the series, Brewers reliever Aaron Ashby has been dominant all postseason, pitching 15.2 innings without allowing a single run. That includes more than three innings of World Series play in which he’s only allowed one hit.
Down 2-0, the highest priced Ray player is Junior Caminero, who is trading around 6% to win the award.

item.title: [Yahoo Sports] Francisco Lindor Wins 2026 Roberto Clemente Award, Continuing a Proud Puerto Rican Legacy
item.dc:creator: Eddie Lennon; Staff Writer
item.description: Francisco Lindor has accomplished just about everything a baseball player could hope to achieve. He's a five-time All-Star, a four-time Silver Slugger and one of the most recognizable shortstops in Major League Baseball. But on October 26, Lindor received an honor that has little to do with his numbers at the plate or his performance on the field. item.content:encoded:
Francisco Lindor has accomplished just about everything a baseball player could hope to achieve. He's a five-time All-Star, a four-time Silver Slugger and one of the most recognizable shortstops in Major League Baseball.
But on October 26, Lindor received an honor that has little to do with his numbers at the plate or his performance on the field.
The New York Mets star was named the 2026 recipient of the Roberto Clemente Award, Major League Baseball's highest individual honor for a player's character, philanthropy and community impact.
For Lindor, the recognition carries an additional layer of meaning. He's a proud Puerto Rican native who grew up learning about Clemente, the legendary Hall of Famer whose impact on baseball extended far beyond the diamond.
Now, Lindor joins the group of players whose actions have helped carry that legacy forward.
Francisco Lindor's Roberto Clemente Award Is About More Than Baseball
The Roberto Clemente Award recognizes the MLB player who best represents baseball through community involvement, philanthropy and positive contributions on and off the field.
Clemente, a 15-time All-Star and one of baseball's greatest players, died on December 31, 1972, while traveling to deliver humanitarian aid to earthquake victims in Nicaragua.
His commitment to helping others became inseparable from his legacy.
For Lindor, that example began long before he reached the Major Leagues.
Growing up in Puerto Rico, he learned about Clemente's career and humanitarian efforts in school. Lindor has spoken about how Clemente inspired him to use his own platform to help others.
Lindor is the fifth Puerto Rican-born player to win the award, joining Edgar Martínez, Carlos Delgado, Carlos Beltrán and Yadier Molina.
That connection makes this recognition particularly significant. Puerto Rico has a rich baseball tradition, and Clemente remains one of its most influential figures. Lindor's award recognizes not only his individual work but also the continuing influence of a Puerto Rican icon whose example transcends generations.
Lindor's Charity Work Starts With Education
One of the clearest examples of Lindor's philanthropy is his commitment to education.
Since 2020, he has donated more than $1 million to Montverde Academy in Florida, his alma mater, helping fund Lindor Hall, a two-story middle school building featuring science and technology laboratories.
He also established the Francisco Lindor Scholarship Fund to help students who otherwise might not have the financial means to attend the school.
His involvement goes beyond writing checks. Lindor remains engaged with students through mentorship, career guidance and youth baseball initiatives.
That commitment reflects an important part of his charitable work: creating opportunities that can continue to benefit young people long after a particular event or donation.
Giving Back to Puerto Rico
Lindor's connection to his home island has also shaped his response to natural disasters.
Following Hurricanes Maria in 2017 and Fiona in 2022, he provided financial support for relief efforts in Puerto Rico. He has also helped restore athletic facilities in his hometown of Caguas and hosted youth baseball clinics.
These efforts connect his philanthropic work to the communities that helped shape him.
For Puerto Rican athletes who reach the highest levels of professional sports, success can provide an opportunity to give back to the places where their journeys began. Lindor has used that opportunity to support recovery efforts, youth development and access to sports.
His work also includes partnerships focused on environmental conservation and ongoing community support.
Making a Difference in Queens
Lindor's impact isn't limited to Puerto Rico or his former school.
In New York, he and his wife, Katia, have supported programs designed to help children and families. Their initiatives include annual back-to-school efforts with New Balance that provide hundreds of students with backpacks and essential school supplies.
Lindor also launched Lindor's Leaders in 2026, a year-long leadership development program for students in Bayside High School's Sports Medicine Program.
The initiative focuses on mental health, communication, teamwork and leadership. Lindor personally mentors participating students, helping them develop skills they can apply in school and throughout their lives.
He has also worked with Children's Miracle Network Hospitals, Special Olympics Florida and organizations supporting youth and families navigating disability.
On the field, Lindor represents the Mets. In the community, his work reaches far beyond the team's fan base.
A $100,000 Boost for the SEEN Foundation
The 2026 award also brings additional support for a cause Lindor and his wife have embraced.
Capital One is donating $100,000 to the SEEN Foundation in honor of Lindor's achievement. The organization works to empower young people, create opportunities and strengthen communities, including supporting families with children navigating physical disabilities.
The contribution gives Lindor's recognition a direct charitable impact, helping support an organization whose mission aligns with the couple's philanthropic efforts.
It's a fitting addition to an award designed not simply to celebrate what a player has done, but to help extend the impact of that work.
Carrying Roberto Clemente's Legacy Forward
There is no shortage of ways to measure Lindor's baseball career. His offensive production, defense, leadership and importance to the Mets will continue to shape how his playing days are remembered.
The Roberto Clemente Award recognizes a different side of that career.
Lindor has invested in education, supported Puerto Rico after devastating hurricanes, mentored students and helped provide opportunities for children and families in New York. These are tangible efforts that extend his influence beyond the ballpark.
His Puerto Rican heritage makes the honor particularly meaningful because Clemente's legacy has long been part of the island's baseball identity. Lindor grew up learning about Clemente's commitment to service, and he now has an opportunity to inspire the next generation in a similar way.
Winning the Roberto Clemente Award is not just another milestone for Francisco Lindor. It's recognition of the person he has chosen to be away from baseball.
For the Mets, Puerto Rico and the broader baseball community, that may be one of his most meaningful accomplishments yet.

item.title: [Sports Illustrated] Breaking Down The Strange, Frustrating 2026 Season of Ketel Marte
item.dc:creator: Alex D'Agostino; Unknown
item.description: There's no question about it. The Arizona Diamondbacks did not get the season they might have hoped for out of star second baseman Ketel Marte. But was he really that bad? In some ways, Marte was better than the numbers showed. On the whole, however, it was one of the worse seasons of his lengthy career. item.content:encoded:
There's no question about it. The Arizona Diamondbacks did not get the season they might have hoped for out of star second baseman Ketel Marte.
But was he really that bad?
In some ways, Marte was better than the numbers showed. On the whole, however, it was one of the worse seasons of his lengthy career. And then, of course, there was all the drama from his no-show at Fenway Park.
So let's break it down.
Was Ketel Marte's 2026 season that bad?
In 2026, Marte hit .249/.316/.432 with 2 homers for a .748 OPS. That would generally be considered a productive season for a major league player, but Marte has set a higher standard for himself.
He produced OPS figures of .893, .932 and .843 in his last three seasons, so 2026 was a big step down, close to the levels of his rough 2022 campaign.
Relatively speaking, it wasn't a good year. But the underlying metrics were not poor. His Baseball Savant page is full of red. Marte hit the ball hard. He was well above average in hard-hit rate (43%), average exit velocity (90.2 MPH) and barrel rate (9.4%). His bat speed ticked up to 74.8 MPH, slightly above 2024 and 2025.
His .280 expected batting average was over 30 points higher than his actual average, and ranked in the 90th percentile. By xwOBA (expected weighted on-base average), he placed in the 85th perceentile with a .349.
Marte rarely whiffed (19.7% whiff rate) and struck out at his lowest clip since 2020 (13.7%). He was worth 2.5 WAR by both Baseball Reference and FanGraphs, and played positive second base defense.
And despite an overall lack of situational proudction from the Diamondbacks, Marte had one of the higher RISP averages on the team. He hit .295 with runners in scoring position and .264 with men on. He also provided a pair of dramatic walk-off home runs.
At the same time, Marte's chase rate rose. He chased outside the strike zone just 24.8% of the time in 2025 — a 71st percentile number — but chased 31.5% of the time in 2026.
He swung early in counts and did not put up the same quality of at-bat he has in the past. He walked at his lowest clip since 2021 (8.2%).
And then, of course, there was the drama.
Ketel Marte's inexcused absence
The situation in late August needs little rehashing for those who paid attention, but Marte was unexpectedly absent from a game against the Red Sox on August 17, which led to a restricted list stint with a personal matter cited as the reasoning.
After days of confusion and drama, Marte sat down with his GM, manager and agent at Salt River Fields. It was determined Marte would go on the IL with a knee injury; he'd then apologize to his teammates and rejoin the club.
All of that came to pass. Though there was lingering frustration, especially given the fact it was not the first time Marte had behaved this way, the team and player seemed to move on.
In actuality, Marte played 141 games, the most since 2023. But shifting focus from his play to his behavior was an objectively rough development for both Marte himself and the team.
It's difficult to suggest his season might have played out vastly different had he chosen to show up in Boston. It's possible.
But Marte has always been an emotional player; when things aren't going well, it can be obvious. He's also had excellent overall seasons in years he has been under scrutiny for this type of behavior.
Ultimately, there's no point in continuing to analyze what happened in the past. But the Diamondbacks are going to have to approach Marte a little differently in this regard going forward, and producing on the field will become even more important for the second baseman.
An Arizona native, Alex D'Agostino is the Publisher and credentialed reporter for Arizona Diamondbacks On SI. He previously served as Deputy Editor for Arizona Diamondbacks and Arizona Cardinals On SI and covered both teams for FanSided. Alex also writes for PHNX Sports. Follow Alex on X/Twitter @AlexDagAZ.
Follow alexdagaz

item.title: [MLB.com] Fiery Caminero airs frustrations about Rays' miscues as focus shifts to Game 3
item.dc:creator: Adam Berry
item.description: MILWAUKEE -- Usually, you’ll see Junior Caminero leading with joy. He’s often the first one out of the dugout, celebrating on the field, when one of his teammates has a big moment. He’s quick to rush to their side to provide consolation. He’s even quicker with a big smile and a gleeful shout. item.content:encoded:
MILWAUKEE -- Usually, you’ll see Junior Caminero leading with joy. He’s often the first one out of the dugout, celebrating on the field, when one of his teammates has a big moment. He’s quick to rush to their side to provide consolation. He’s even quicker with a big smile and a gleeful shout.
But he showed a different side of his emerging leadership after the sixth inning in Game 2 of the World Series on Saturday night at American Family Field. After seeing the uncharacteristically sloppy Rays blow a four-run lead in an eventual 5-4 loss to the Brewers, Caminero was caught by television cameras shouting at his teammates in the dugout.
“Trying to help the team. Trying to help the team and get our heads up, right?” Caminero said afterward through interpreter Kevin Vera. “Just trying to create some energy and get some life back into us.”
Speaking in front of his locker more than half an hour after Yandy Díaz struck out against Aaron Ashby to end the game, Caminero was clearly still frustrated by his team’s overall performance as the Rays fell into a 2-0 hole.
Asked if he had seen something specific that he didn’t like, leading to his emotional display in the dugout, Caminero responded quickly with a reference to the Rays’ multiple uncharacteristic misplays in the field.
“We had to get outs. In that moment, we weren't doing our job, and against Milwaukee, if you give up outs, they're gonna do that,” Caminero said. “They're gonna use that against you, and that's what happens. So I was trying to say the message [that], 'Hey, we've got to get outs.'”
Caminero also credited the Brewers, acknowledging that the National League champions have “played really well.” And he was optimistic that the Rays would get back to their style of play after being thrust into the World Series spotlight in a raucous environment the past two nights.
“Some players haven't played at this stage, and I understand maybe the pressure that they might feel. Me personally, I've played at similar stages at this point in my career, so I feel comfortable in certain ways,” Caminero said. “We've just got to win. We've just got to do our thing to flip the page, have a fresh mind on Monday and win Game 3.”
Caminero played a part in the Rays’ four-run rally in the first inning, smacking a single to left field that gave them a 2-0 lead, then scoring on Liam Hicks’ two-run homer off Brewers starter Logan Henderson. But Milwaukee kept Tampa Bay’s All-Star third baseman off the basepaths the rest of the night, and the Rays didn’t score again after the first.
That opened the door for the Brewers to come back. So did Tampa Bay’s mistakes on the mound, at the plate, on the bases and in the field.
“That’s the game, right? I guarantee you one thing, that nobody in this clubhouse wants to play the baseball that we've played the last couple days. That's not who we are,” Caminero said. “But at the end of the day, we've played the game in the last two days, and this is the type of baseball that's unfolded. So, it's the game. It's unfortunate.
“We can sit on it tonight, but the rest of the way, it's a new day. It's a new game, and yeah, we look forward to Game 3.”
Caminero had already taken it a step further earlier in his postgame interview, saying the Rays can’t afford to lose another game after the series resumes on Monday night at Tropicana Field.
“They were close, but look, we've got to win,” he said. “The rest of the way, they're mandatory that we've got to win.
“Just go on Monday with a fresh mind, fresh start on Monday and see what happens.”
Caminero attempted to exemplify that as the postgame scrum broke up around his locker, saying, “I already forgot about these last two days. The series now, in my mind, starts on Monday.”

item.content:encoded:
The New York Yankees are coming off another strong regular season.
That said, they also had another letdown in the postseason.
After sweeping the Boston Red Sox in the Wild Card Series, the Yankees got swept by the Tampa Bay Rays in the ALDS.
They lost the final game (at home in the Bronx) by a score of 4-3.
New York Yankees Will Pay 34-Year-Old $27 Million
With the season over, it’s worth taking a look at Carlos Rodon.
The 33-year-old (who will turn 34 in December) is coming off a strong regular season.
He went 7-3 with a 2.67 ERA in 16 starts.
Chris Kirschner of The Athletic wrote (on September 16): “Carlos Rodón, who regained some velocity as his outing progressed, has not allowed more than three runs in 25 straight starts. It is the longest streak in Yankees history and tied for the sixth-longest streak in MLB history.”
Carlos Rodon #55 of the New York Yankees delivers a pitch in the first inning against the New York Mets at Yankee Stadium on September 11, 2026 in The Bronx borough of New York City. The New York Yankees and the New York Mets are wearing hats to honor first responders on the 25th anniversary of the 9/11 attack on New York during the game.
It’s also worth mentioning that the Yankees still owe Rodon a lot of money.
He will be paid $27 million during the 2027 season (h/t Spotrac).
ESPN’s Jeff Passan wrote (on December 15, 2022): “Left-hander Carlos Rodón and the New York Yankees are in agreement on a six-year, $162 million contract, sources familiar with the deal tell ESPN.”
Rodon will become a free agent following the 2028 MLB season.
Looking At Rodon
Carlos Rodon #55 of the New York Yankees pitches in the fourth inning against the Baltimore Orioles at Oriole Park at Camden Yards on August 18, 2026 in Baltimore, Maryland.
Rodon was picked in the 1st round of the 2014 MLB Draft.
He spent the first seven years of his career playing for the Chicago White Sox.
After Chicago, Rodon (who is a three-time MLB All-Star) had a quick stint with the San Francisco Giants.
Samantha Busch, Ashley Rodón and Carlos Rodón attend the Carlos Rodón Foundation 2026 Willow Gala at the Refinery on August 24, 2026 in Brooklyn, New York.
Rodon has 100 career wins with a 3.67 ERA.

item.content:encoded:
Brewers' Jacob Misiorowski's pre-Game 2 routine? Trading Pokémon cards with fans appeared first on ClutchPoints. Add ClutchPoints as a Preferred Source by clicking here.
Manager Pat Murphy's Milwaukee Brewers made history in Game 1 of the World Series, scoring a win over the Tampa Bay Rays by a score of 3-2 behind ace hurler Jacob Misiorowski. The Brewers planned to send Logan Henderson to the mound for Game 2 giving Misiorowski a chance to relax beforehand.
The Brewers star was spotted near the dugout, as shared by MLB Network's Jon Heyman, as he began trading Pokemon cards with a young fan.
Misiorowski has become a favorite player for fans of all ages as he has led the Brewers to huge win after huge win, including a sweep over the back-to-back defending champion Los Angeles Dodgers in the NLCS. Misiorowski made World Series history on his first pitch of Game 1, scorching the radar gun with a fastball that looked like something out of a Disney movie.
The Brewers' starting pitching was seen as lacking depth compared to the Rays heading into the World Series, but Misiorwoski did his job, giving way to Henderson for Game 2 at American Family Field in Milwaukee. Henderson has compiled statistics in recent games that have given the Brewers confidence that he can lead his team to victory.
The Brewers' home ballpark can hold nearly 42,000 fans, and they appear united behind their team in pursuit of their first-ever World Series championship. Misiorowski might not get the chance to pitch for Murphy's team for a few games, but he is clearly making the most of his time in the fall classic as fans continue to enjoy the ride headed deep into October.
Related: Former MVP Ryan Braun gets completely real on Brewers' World Series vs. Rays
Related: Brewers make World Series Game 3 starting pitching decision

Joe Girardi of the New York Yankees was the last player to achiev
item.content:encoded:
William Contreras was undoubtedly the Milwaukee Brewers MVP in Game 1 of the World Series.
Contreras had an RBI single in the first inning, a walk in the sixth inning and another base hit in the eighth inning. Defensively, he caught two runners stealing to end innings and won two ABS challenges.
He became the best catcher this century to have multiple caught stealings and hits in a World Series game, per MLB Network's Sarah Langs. Joe Girardi of the New York Yankees was the last player to achieve that feat.
Girardi did it in Game 3 of the 1999 World Series against the Atlanta Braves. It had been 27 years since a catcher had a game like that, and Contreras seemed due to break the drought.
He was the best catcher in the regular season at catching runners, and the Tampa Bay Rays are a team that likes to run. Something had to give, and it was Contreras who came out on top.
At the plate, he continued a red-hot October, and the Brewers will need him to continue his hitting ways for the rest of the series. The Brewers can go up 2-0 on the Rays on Saturday, and if Contreras is swinging the bat as he has been, there is really no pitcher who is going to give him problems.
The Rays are expected to stay aggressive on the basepaths, so Contreras' arm will continue to be tested. In Game 1, he changed the complexion of the game by erasing baserunners, and could do the same in Game 2.
More MLB: Brewers Pitcher Close To Breaking Andrew Miller's MLB Record

item.title: [House That Hank Built] Matt Olson’s Fielding Bible win puts Braves first baseman in rare company
item.dc:creator: Steven Teal
item.description: Award season is upon us, and the Atlanta Braves have already secured some hardware. It stinks not to see the team in the playoffs, but there were some great performances shown to fans this season. item.content:encoded:
Award season is upon us, and the Atlanta Braves have already secured some hardware. It stinks not to see the team in the playoffs, but there were some great performances shown to fans this season. Matt Olson was unsurprisingly among the players who gave fans something to cheer about. His time at the plate was inconsistent at times, but he still put up respectable numbers.
Atlanta's first baseman had a .251/.321/.502 slash line, with 34 doubles, 41 home runs, 93 RBI, and a 122 wRC+. Those are great numbers, but he disappeared in the postseason, which was tough to watch. The offense is one aspect of Olson's impressive game, but his defense remained elite in 2026. His impressive fielding work led to his first award of the season. Olson was awarded a Fielding Bible Award to recognize him as the best defensive first baseman in baseball.
The Fielding Bible Awards are handed out each season to one player at each of the nine positions as the top fielder in MLB at that position. They also award one "multi-position" player, one overall Defensive Player of the Year, and a Defensive Team of the Year. Recipients are voted on by a panel of experts based on a combination of stats, the eye test, and any other factors the voters choose to consider.
Matt Olson's latest defensive honor a reminder of his underrated skill set
Olson was in a tight race with Padres first baseman Ty France this season. However, his incredible OAA and FRV set him apart. He finished the season with an 11 outs above average (OAA) and 12 fielding run value (FRV). Those numbers were both the best in baseball among all first basemen. France edged out Olson in defensive runs saved (DRS), with 15 DRS compared to Olson's 11 DRS.
This win was Olson's sixth Fielding Bible Award at first base, which surpassed Albert Pujols for the most wins at the position. Atlanta's lefty slugger is now tied with Yadier Molina and Andrelton Simmons for the second-most all-time wins among all positions. Olson only trails Mookie Betts, who has seven wins, for the most Fielding Bible Awards.
It likely won't be the last award for Olson, who is also nominated for a Gold Glove Award this season. He continues to be a wonderful addition for the Braves.

item.content:encoded:
Former Toronto Blue Jays pitcher Kevin Gausman was rumored to return in free agency. He was traded to the Chicago Cubs on Aug. 2.
Toronto received outfielder Brett Bateman and infielder Ty Southisene. Gausman was in the final year of a five-year, $110 million contract.
Now that the regular season has ended, rumors started swirling about a potential Gausman return due to his personal connection with the team and the city. He helped the Blue Jays reach the World Series last year. He went 5-10 with a 4.38 ERA in 23 starts for Toronto in 2026.
But despite Gausman’s wishes, the team does not plan on that, which has now forced the 35-year-old to move on as well.
Kevin Gausman’s $7.6 Million News Emerges
Gausman has put his Toronto home on the market this week with Harvey Kalles Real Estate for $6.885 million.
He bought the property in March 2022 for $7.65 million. The asking price sits $765,000 below that figure.
The house sits in Lytton Park, a Toronto neighborhood. It has six bedrooms, seven bathrooms and nearly 5,000 square feet, Blue Jays Insider reported. It was built in 2019.
The listing highlights a chef’s kitchen, a family room, a heated driveway and a south-facing backyard. The primary bedroom has a five-piece en suite bathroom and a walk-in closet. The family lived there for about four and a half years.
Gausman had not listed the house in the weeks after the trade. Reports in early October pointed to that as a possible sign of a return. The Athletic reported that a reunion with Toronto seemed likely if Gausman keeps playing.
Before the trade, Gausman told Sportsnet the family would leave Toronto after 2026. He was already preparing for a future out of the city.
Kevin Gausman Has Spoken Warmly About Toronto Since the Trade
Gausman said on the Baseball Isn’t Boring podcast that Toronto “was my second home.” He added that the family had a home there and that leaving was hard.
After his last Blue Jays start on Aug. 1, Gausman called signing with Toronto the best decision he ever made.
His wife, Taylor, wrote on Instagram on Aug. 3 that choosing Toronto was the family’s best decision. She wrote that the couple’s daughters grew up there. She declined to say goodbye and offered a see-you-later instead.
In March, Gausman said his family loved the city’s parks, its summers and its people. He said they also loved their house and neighborhood.
As he left the clubhouse after the trade, Gausman recalled his younger daughter’s first birthday party in the backyard. He also recalled a photo of both girls on the front step the week the family bought the house.
Gausman has said he hopes to show his daughters around Canada after he retires. He also wants to take them to Blue Jays games, MLB Trade Rumors reported. He said on the 6ix Inning Stretch podcast that he plans to return to Toronto after retiring.

item.title: [trentonian.com] World Series: Brewers withstand Rays’ comeback attempt to win Game 1
item.dc:creator: Steve Megargee

item.content:encoded:
MILWAUKEE (AP) — Trevor Megill was shouting in celebration and the Milwaukee Brewers were bolting out of the dugout to congratulate one another, believing they had just escaped a ninth-inning jam to win Game 1 of the World Series.
Not quite yet.
What initially was ruled a game-ending double play got overturned after a video review showed Brewers shortstop Cooper Pratt’s right foot was slightly off the bag when he reached to catch a high throw from second baseman Brice Turang.
No problem.
Megill regrouped and struck out Jonny DeLuca with two runners in scoring position as Milwaukee edged the Tampa Bay Rays 3-2 on Friday night.
“It’s good to get the first win out of the way,” Megill said. “That’s where all the nerves are at. First game, a lot of anticipation and build-up to where we are right now.”
The ninth inning was particularly nerve-racking for the Brewers and the sellout crowd attending Milwaukee’s first World Series game since 1982.
“You have a big range of emotions,” said team captain Christian Yelich, whose RBI triple in the first put the Brewers ahead for good. “It’s a big credit to Trev for locking back in right there and making some huge pitches after you have that emotional dump and then have to get back on it.”
Tampa Bay trailed 3-1 and hadn’t put a runner on since the sixth until it mounted its comeback attempt against Megill.
Jonathan Aranda, who went 3 for 3 with a walk, and Chandler Simpson hit consecutive one-out singles. A double steal involving pinch-runner Jorge Mateo and Simpson put runners on second and third before Junior Caminero walked on a 3-2 pitch in the dirt to load the bases.
Liam Hicks hit a grounder to the right side, and Turang ranged well to his left to field the ball before throwing to Pratt to start what initially was called a 4-6-3 double play.
Fireworks went off, players poured onto the field and Milwaukee fans roared. But then the crowd hushed as it watched the play again on the videoboard.
“You’ve got to think worst-case scenario there,” Megill said. “I thought the challenge was at first base, maybe a bobble or something. But it was pretty clear once the replay went up that it was on the play at second base. Zoomed in and it didn’t look good. It’s all right. We picked up Cooper there. He’ll pick us up tomorrow.”
The out call at second was changed to safe by umpire Alfonso Márquez at the MLB Replay Center, which caught Pratt by surprise.
“Obviously, it was close,” the 22-year-old rookie said. “I just didn’t think it was enough to overturn, so I wasn’t thinking anything of it. The video I saw, thought my cleat was dragging. … There must have been some other angles that I haven’t seen. It ultimately didn’t matter because we won.”
The Brewers won because Megill got DeLuca to swing and miss at a 2-2 pitch, capping a night in which Tampa Bay went 0 for 6 with runners in scoring position.
“This is an extremely confident group,” Rays manager Kevin Cash said. “You know that. We know that. They’re going to be fine. I think the frustration comes from we were one swing of the bat away right at the end of potentially taking the lead.”
The Game 1 winner has gone on to win the World Series 62.8% of the time.
This marks the first World Series featuring two teams seeking their first championship since 1980, when the Philadelphia Phillies beat the Kansas City Royals in six games. The only other major league clubs without a World Series title are the Colorado Rockies, San Diego Padres and Seattle Mariners.
Milwaukee took a 2-0 lead in the first inning against Nick Martinez. NL Cy Young Award favorite Jacob Misiorowski allowed one run and four hits over five innings to help the Brewers stay in front before relievers Abner Uribe and Aaron Ashby shut down the Rays through the eighth.
Misiorowski, who had a season-low three strikeouts, opened the game with a 103.5 mph fastball — the fastest pitch ever thrown in a World Series.
“The adrenaline kind of took over, and I tensed up and threw it hard,” said Misiorowski, who earned the win. “Then I settled down, and that was the game plan, to settle in and do me. Don’t try and overdo it.”
Milwaukee’s Jackson Chourio and William Contreras each had two hits, including an RBI single. Contreras also threw out two runners trying to steal.
Tampa Bay managed to hang around thanks in part to Martinez, who gave up those two runs in the first but held Milwaukee scoreless through the rest of his five-inning stint. The Brewers added an insurance run in the seventh when Chourio singled home Pratt.
Then came all the action in the ninth, with the Brewers’ premature celebration followed by a team-wide sigh of relief as Pratt offered some parting words to Megill.
“I just said, ‘Thank you, man. Thanks for picking me up,’” Pratt said. “That’s what this game is. It’s a game of pick-me-up. He picked me up today.”
Up next
Drew Rasmussen (16-5, 2.67 ERA) pitches for Tampa Bay and Logan Henderson (11-3, 2.47) starts for Milwaukee in Game 2 on Saturday night. In this postseason, Rasmussen is 2-0 with a 1.29 ERA and Henderson is 0-0 with a 3.00 ERA.

item.content:encoded:
La Serie Mundial 2026 apenas está por comenzar y el dominicano de los Rays, Junior Caminero, ya dio una muestra del poder que tiene en su madero al dañar la pantalla gigante del American Family Field, el estadio de los Brewers, donde se llevará a cabo el Juego 1 por el título de las Grandes Ligas de Béisbol (MLB).
El jueves por la noche, durante la práctica previa al primer desafío, Caminero conectó un batazo que fue a estrellarse contra la pantalla gigante; el panel de la jumbotron, que proyectaba el logo del Clásico de Otoño, quedó inservible por el resto de la práctica de bateo.
Junior Caminero's homer knocked out the lights on the American Family Field scoreboard ???? pic.twitter.com/pabSVoNloy
— MLB (@MLB) October 23, 2026
Caminero podría ser una de las piezas clave en el desarrollo de esta Serie Mundial, más aún llegando encendido tras su actuación en el Juego 6 de la Serie de Campeonato ante los Guardians, cuando disparó un jonrón contra el poste del jardín izquierdo durante la séptima entrada, produciendo las dos carreras que ampliaron definitivamente la delantera de los Rays.
Si la muestra del jueves por la noche es un anticipo de lo que puede hacer, Junior Caminero está listo para dejar su huella en esta Serie Mundial.

item.title: [dairylandexpress.com] Pat Murphy throws the Rays a curveball with Brewers' batting order in World Series Game 1
item.dc:creator: Dylan Carter
item.description: If you expected the Milwaukee Brewers to enter the World Series without making any adjustments, you must not have been watching the team this season. Even after sweeping the Los Angeles Dodgers in the NLCS and overcoming a red-hot Padres squad in the Division Series, manager Pat Murphy is always finding new ways to keep his opponents on their toes. The Brewers released their batting order on Friday afternoon, just hours before first pitch. Their updated order will be as follows: 1. Jackson Chour
item.content:encoded:
If you expected the Milwaukee Brewers to enter the World Series without making any adjustments, you must not have been watching the team this season. Even after sweeping the Los Angeles Dodgers in the NLCS and overcoming a red-hot Padres squad in the Division Series, manager Pat Murphy is always finding new ways to keep his opponents on their toes.
The Brewers released their batting order on Friday afternoon, just hours before first pitch. Their updated order will be as follows:
1. Jackson Chourio
2. Jake Bauers
3. Christian Yelich
4. William Contreras
5. Brice Turang
6. Garrett Mitchell
7. Cooper Pratt
8. Sal Frelick
9. David Hamilton
What should we take away from the Milwaukee Brewers' updated batting order for Game 1 of the World Series?
This new-look order should give the Brewers an interesting dynamic of staggering lefty and righty batters, likely in hopes of keeping Game 1 starter Nick Martinez, a righty, out of a consistent rhythm to begin the contest. By moving Contreras to fourth, it sets up Milwaukee's best home run hitter this postseason for a grand slam opportunity, should it arise. Meanwhile, Yelich at the third spot gives the Brew Crew a likely opportunity for some much-needed contact hitting early in the rotation.
It's far from surprising to see first baseman Jake Bauers taking such a firm position near the top of the batting order, as Bauers emerged as one of the most reliable offensive threats on the team, and frankly, in all of baseball. His ability to extend the pitch count and make contact persistently has been a thorn in the sides of pitchers everywhere, so this is likely Murphy's best attempt to extend Martinez's pitch count early.
Meanwhile, Turang slotting back into the fifth spot in the lineup makes sense given his inconsistent production thus far in the postseason. Through eight games, the 26-year-old is hitting just .222 with six hits to seven strikeouts. The good news, however, is that Turang turned a corner in the Dodgers series, logging hits in three of four hits, while scoring a run in each contest.
The end of the lineup should be of interest as well. All year long, Brewers fans grappled with questions over David Hamilton's place in the lineup, but through the postseason, he's certainly proving he belongs. Milwaukee is in serious need of some production late in the order, so all eyes will be on Hamilton, as well as Cooper Pratt and Sal Frelick, to carry that torch.
Overall, this is a wise move by Pat Murphy to make sure his lineup isn't identical to what Tampa Bay was expecting to see. Although the players are the same, a little shake-up in the order might force Martinez and the Rays' defense to think twice, which is all the Brewers can really ask for in a matchup of two teams that are this talented defensively.

item.content:encoded:
Jonathan Aranda has become a pivotal player for the Tampa Bay Rays.
By the end of the regular season, he had the second-most homers (22) in the franchise, behind Junior Caminero (42).
Before he enters the 2026 World Series, let’s learn five fast facts about his wife, who has watched him grow in his career.
1. They Got Married in 2025
On Oct. 24, 2025, the pair got married.
This means their first anniversary will take place during the World Series this year — a rare way to celebrate.
2. She Threw a Ceremonial First Pitch
On May 16, 2026, Milka threw the first pitch for Tampa Bay’s clash against the Miami Marlins at Tropicana Field.
Unfortunately, the Rays ended up facing a 10-5 loss to the Marlins that day, but they did end up winning the three-game series.
3. They Have a Daughter
Jonathan and Milka have a 2-year-old daughter named Regina.
Following her birth, he discussed how being a father has changed him.
“It’s definitely changed a little bit,” he said, per Adam Berry of MLB.com. “Now it’s a little easier because now I’m doing everything for her and our family.”
During that conversation, he also joked about having newfound “dad strength.”
4. Milka Is From Mexico
Not only is Jonathan from Mexico, but so is his wife.
Jonathan became the first Mexican-born first baseman, and they now proudly instill their culture in their daughter.
5. She Was With Jonathan Long Before He Exploded in the Big Leagues
Their early relationship was kept fairly quiet, but she has had the opportunity to watch him grow into the elite hitter he is today.
During the regular season, he slashed .274/.358/.434with a .792 OPS and a career-high 22 homers through 155 games.
Their marriage remains relatively private.
Where Do the Rays Stand Ahead of Game 1?
ST PETERSBURG, FLORIDA – SEPTEMBER 2: Jonathan Aranda #8 of the Tampa Bay Rays at bat in the bottom of the first inning against the New York Mets at Tropicana Field on September 2, 2026 in St Petersburg, Florida. (Photo by Parker S. Freedman/Getty Images)
Tampa Bay enters the World Series as an underdog.
The Brewers appear to hold a slight edge over the Rays, but this isn’t shocking considering they led the majors 103-59 overall during the regular season.
Tampa Bay dominated during the ALDS and the ALCS, leading up to the moment they’ve been waiting for — a run in the Fall Classic.
KANSAS CITY, MISSOURI – JUNE 24: Manager Kevin Cash #16 of the Tampa Bay Rays talks with reporters prior to a game against the Kansas City Royals at Kauffman Stadium on June 24, 2025 in Kansas City, Missouri. (Photo by Ed Zurga/Getty Images)
There’s always a chance they could upset Milwaukee, but doing so will be on easy feat.

item.title: [Heavy.com] Paige Almendariz, Christian Yelich's Girlfriend: 5 Fast Facts You Need to Know
item.dc:creator: Cole Sullivan
item.description: The World Series will be historic no matter how it plays out, as neither the Milwaukee Brewers nor the Tampa Bay Rays have ever won a championship. While the series means a lot to everyone competing, it could be a special moment for former NL MVP Christian Yelich. He’s in his 14th season and will have his first opportunity to play for a World Series title. One of his biggest supporters over the next few weeks will be his girlfriend, Paige Almendariz. Here are five interesting facts about their r
item.content:encoded:
The World Series will be historic no matter how it plays out, as neither the Milwaukee Brewers nor the Tampa Bay Rays have ever won a championship.
While the series means a lot to everyone competing, it could be a special moment for former NL MVP Christian Yelich. He’s in his 14th season and will have his first opportunity to play for a World Series title.
One of his biggest supporters over the next few weeks will be his girlfriend, Paige Almendariz.
Here are five interesting facts about their relationship together.
Who Is Almendariz?
Like Yelich, Almendariz is a professional athlete in her own right. She currently plays defender for DC Power in the USL Super League.
The 29-year-old was born and raised in Sacramento, California, and has developed into a successful soccer player. Throughout her career, she has also played for clubs in Portugal, including Benfica and Braga, and won multiple titles. Now, Yelich will try to add a championship of his own.
How Did Almendariz and Yelich First Meet?
The two have kept their relationship relatively private, but they reportedly began dating in late 2025 and made their romance public through social media.
Almendariz has continuously shared photos of herself, Yelich and her dog on several occasions.
Check it out:
They Are Both California Natives
As mentioned, Almendariz is from California, and so is Yelich. He was born and raised in Thousand Oaks and attended Thousand Oaks High School.
However, they grew up roughly 400 miles apart, with West Sacramento, where Almendariz grew up, about a seven-hour drive from Thousand Oaks.
Yelich graduated from high school in 2010, while Almendariz graduated in 2016.
They Were Both Division I College Athletes
Both were Division I athletes, although Yelich took a different path when it came to his college commitment.
Out of high school, he committed to play baseball at the University of Miami, a long way from California. However, after the Florida Marlins drafted him, he elected to sign with the MLB team and turn pro immediately. That decision ultimately worked out, given the career he’s had.
As for Almendariz, she enrolled at UNLV to play college soccer after graduating as the valedictorian of her class, staying relatively close to home.
She was a standout defender for the university from 2016 to 2019 before heading to Portugal in 2020 to sign with Lank Vilaverdense.
They Both Have Athletic Siblings
Athletics run in both families. Yelich’s younger brother, Collin, was drafted by the Atlanta Braves in 2015 and played professional baseball for several years, while his other brother, Cameron, served in the United States Marine Corps.
Almendariz is one of five sisters, and her sister Brittany also played Division I soccer at UNLV as a defender. The two even shared the field when Paige was a freshman.

item.content:encoded:
Mets still have serious first base problem after Pete Alonso signed with Orioles originally appeared on The Sporting News. Add The Sporting News as a Preferred Source by clicking here.
Last offseason, the New York Mets opted not to re-sign Pete Alonso, as the first baseman signed with the Baltimore Orioles.
It's safe to say the Mets probably regret that decision, as their offense could've used the 43 home runs and 113 RBIs Alonso produced in 2026.
Jorge Polanco, Alonso's replacement, played just 37 games and had -1.4 bWAR before season-ending ankle surgery in August.
For the Mets to achieve an "A+" offseason, they must address their first base problem, FanSided's Zachary Rotman wrote.
"Letting Pete Alonso walk in free agency was a decision that made sense given how power-hitting first basemen over 30 tend to age historically, but it also required the Mets to find an adequate replacement.
"Given the fact that their first basemen ranked 29th in the Majors with an 85 wRC+ and dead last with -1.4 fWAR in 2026, it's clear that [David] Stearns did not do a good enough job in that area," Rotman wrote.
One player the Mets could target is Teruaki Sato, who won the Triple Crown in Nippon Professional Baseball.
The worst-case scenario is if the Mets have Jared Young as their everyday starter on Opening Day.
"Jared Young as a platoon option at first base is fine enough, but the Mets either need to acquire a good right-handed bat to pair with him against left-handed pitchers or acquire a legitimate every-day starter — whether that's Teruaki Sato in free agency or someone else via trade. It's hard to field a potent offense if you get nothing out of the first base position," Rotman added.
Given how poorly New York's first basemen hit in 2026, adding a veteran right-handed hitter or someone like Sato should be a top priority this offseason.

item.content:encoded:
Why Rays' key to World Series victory might revolve around Jacob Misiorowski originally appeared on The Sporting News. Add The Sporting News as a Preferred Source by clicking here.
The Tampa Bay Rays are facing the Milwaukee Brewers in the 2026 MLB World Series, and after the Brewers swept the reining champions in four games in the NLCS, the Brewers are favorites in this matchup.
They also have home-field advantage, which makes the Rays' task a lot harder. But there's certainly a path for the Rays to win it all. But how can they actually win the World Series?
ESPN's Alden Gonzalez highlighted how the Brewers have a vulnerable starting rotation, led by Jacob Misiorowski, and that if the Rays can chase him out of the game early, the Rays could be set up for a lot of success in the World Series.
Rays can beat Brewers by getting after Jacob Misiorowski
"To beat the Brewers, you have to take advantage of their starting rotation," Gonzalez writes. "It begins with running up the pitch counts of their two front-line starters, Jacob Misiorowski and Logan Henderson."
If the Rays are able to make the Brewers' top-two starting pitchers throw a lot of pitches early in games, making it so they don't last long in their respective starts, they can have a real chance of winning it all.
It might seem like a simple thing to chase a pitcher early, but considering the Brewers' top-heavy bullpen, getting to the middle of the bullpen might prove to be a key to this series.
Besides, in Games 3 and 4, Milwaukee will be relying on more of their bullpen, with starters Dustin May, Shane Drohan, and Robert Gasser set to be involved.
If the Rays can force the Brewers to the bullpen early in Games 1 and 2, they could set themselves up nicely for the rest of the series.
As Gonzalez put it, "scoring early will be a must for the Rays." They can win the World Series even if they struggle against Misiorowski and Henderson, but if they have success against them, their odds of winning the series will increase significantly.
The snowball effect of chasing Misiorowski and/or Henderson from a game early would be huge. Taxing the Brewers' bullpen is the key to the Rays' success, and to do so, they're going to have to get after Misiorowski.
Games 1 and 2 might be a telling outcome for how the series will go. If the Rays can tax the bullpens, they could be set up for success once the series heads to Tampa Bay.
They'll need their own pitchers to play great, but if the Rays' offense can force the pitch counts of Henderson and Misiorowski to go high early in their respective starts, they could be set up for success in the World Series against the Brewers.

item.content:encoded:
The New York Yankees will have a lot of decisions to make over the winter.
One of them will be the upcoming free agency of Paul Goldschmidt.
He is coming off his second season playing for the franchise.
Goldschmidt finished the year batting batting .252 with 87 hits, 18 home runs, 52 RBIs, 44 runs and one stolen base in 105 games.
Despite turning 39 in September, he was a very reliable player.
The Yankees wrote (via X) on August 7: “Congratulations to Paul Goldschmidt on being named our 2026 @MLBPAA Heart & Hustle Award Winner 👏”
Yankees Cutting Ties With 7x All-Star Would Me A Mistake
Goldschmidt could likely be signed to another one-year deal that would not lead to any risk for the Yankees.
He is a solid (and well liked) veteran who can still help the team compete for a World Series in 2027.
@eyyankees wrote (on October 8): “39 year old Paul Goldschmidt: Paul Goldschmidt suggested he would like to keep playing. Solid Yankee. Thankful for his years here.”

item.title: [CBS Sports] The state of the outfield position heading into 2027: Pete Crow-Armstrong leads a talented but thin field
