item.content:encoded:
The Milwaukee Brewers don't have to reveal their National League Division Series roster until Saturday morning, but the organization gave a positive update on Friday ahead of the official announcement.
Throughout the week, the guy to watch from an injury perspective has been infielder Joey Ortiz. The 28-year-old has been dealing with knee and abdominal injuries, but is trending in the right direction. Brewers manager Pat Murphy said so himself on Friday and noted that the expectation is that he will be good to go for the National League Division Series.
"It looks like it's progressing in the right direction," Murphy said. "He's still ... he still has some pain. He's going to tell you, 'no,' and all that kind of stuff. He wants to play very badly. I would say at this point, we are planning on him being available."
Joey Ortiz Is Going To Be Alright
There was a point during the 2026 season in which this update wouldn't have moved the needle much for Milwaukee. But things are certainly different now. Before he shifted from shortstop to third base, Ortiz was really struggling offensively. He was batting .207 with one home run and 14 RBIs in 60 games before Cooper Pratt made his big league debut. Pratt made his debut on June 16, which shifted Ortiz's role away from shortstop.
Things changed for the better for Ortiz afterward. From June 17 through the end of the season, Ortiz slashed .310/.348/.491 with an .840 OPS, eight home runs, 33 RBIs, nine doubles and four triples in 74 games.
He went from being someone at risk of being sent down to the minors, to being integral to this club's success down the stretch. Fortunately, when the Brewers open up National League Division Series play on Saturday, the current expectation is that Ortiz will be in the mix, barring some sort of last-second setback.
The Brewers have a tough series ahead. The San Diego Padres are the hottest team in baseball and aren't going to be an easy out. For the Brewers to win, they're going to need all of the help that they can get. So, this update is very positive for the organization heading into their most important series of the season so far. If the Brewers can take down the Padres in the NLDS, they would advance to face either the Los Angeles Dodgers or the Atlanta Braves in the National League Championship Series.
Patrick McAvoy's experiences include local and national sports coverage at the New England Sports Network with a focus on baseball and basketball. Outside of journalism, Patrick received an MBA at Brandeis University. For all business/marketing inquiries regarding "Milwaukee Brewers On SI," please reach out to Scott Neville: scott@moreviewsmedia.com

item.dc:creator: Dallin Ballard

item.content:encoded:
Alex Bregman has officially won the 2026 Rizzo Award, but the victory was far from a blowout. According to Bleed Cubbie Blue, the new third baseman finished with a score of +26, just a half point ahead of Pete Crow-Armstrong. This marks the closest finish in the entire 13-year history of the award. The race was so tight that fans could only guess the winner until the very end of the season.
The Numbers That Tell the Story
The final standings show a massive gap between the top performers and the rest of the roster. Bregman led all free agent signings with his +26 mark, proving he was the most impactful new addition. Per Bleed Cubbie Blue, Crow-Armstrong followed closely with +25.5 as the top returning player. Ben Brown sat at +13.5, while the legendary Ian Happ and Aaron Civale both finished with +10. The top ten list is packed with talent, but the battle for first place was a genuine nail-biter.
At the other end of the spectrum, the bottom of the list tells a different story about the team's struggles. Nico Hoerner finished with -18, while Dansby Swanson landed at -17. Seiya Suzuki also ended up at -17, joining the group of players who had a rough season. The data shows a clear divide between the heroes who carried the team and the goats who dragged it down. Even the best teams have players who simply cannot find their footing when it matters most.
Why the Playoffs Changed Everything
The regular season heroics did not translate into a deep playoff run for the Cubs. The team was swept by the Padres in the Wild Card series, ending the season with barely a whimper. Bleed Cubbie Blue noted that the Cubs looked completely overmatched over those two days.
Despite the loss, the regular season data suggests the team was built to hit home runs. For almost the whole year, the roster stayed close to the top of the home run leaders. However, the playoffs exposed a lack of pitching depth that the regular season stats could not hide. The Padres had a clear plan and executed it perfectly against Cubs starter Matthew Boyd. They swung early and often, recognizing strikes and punishing mistakes. The Cubs needed a pitcher who could go seven innings against a good offense, and they simply did not have one.
Bregman's regular season success stands as a bright spot in an otherwise painful year. His +26 score proves he was the right choice for the club, even if the playoffs did not go as planned. The question now is whether the team can build on this individual success or if the roster needs a complete overhaul. The numbers do not lie about who helped the most, but the final score of the season remains the same. The Cubs are back to square one.

item.title: [MLB.com] Here's how the pitching might line up for the White Sox-Guardians ALDS
item.dc:creator: Tim Stebbins; Scott Merkin
item.description: CLEVELAND -- While battling for the American League Central title last month, the Guardians and White Sox divisional race featured an added reward: a first-round bye in the postseason that would allow the champ to set its preferred pitching plan for the AL Division Series. item.content:encoded:
CLEVELAND -- While battling for the American League Central title last month, the Guardians and White Sox divisional race featured an added reward: a first-round bye in the postseason that would allow the champ to set its preferred pitching plan for the AL Division Series.
That’s where we find ourselves now, as Cleveland and Chicago get set for their first-ever playoff matchup.
As the AL Central champion Guardians enjoyed a bye this week, they also lined up their staff anchors for the first two games of ALDS, which is set to kick off with Game 1 on Saturday at Progressive Field. Meanwhile, the White Sox are working through things after they completed a sweep of the Astros in the best-of-three AL Wild Card Series on Wednesday to advance.
Chicago’s plan, understandably, is less settled coming off its Wild Card series, though Cleveland has some uncertainty as well. What could the pitching matchups look like? Let’s take a look.
Guardians
Messick has come a long way in one year. The lefty wasn’t on the Guardians’ roster in the 2025 AL Wild Card Series, following his seven-start debut stint in the Majors down the stretch. This spring, he had to earn a spot on Cleveland’s Opening Day roster. Now, the Guards are hoping he paves the way as they push for October glory.
Messick’s stellar rookie season could make him a finalist for both the AL Cy Young Award and the Rookie of the Year Award. The 25-year-old had a 2.56 ERA (seventh in MLB) in 186 1/3 innings over 32 starts, with 193 strikeouts and 49 walks. In perhaps a good omen, he was particularly effective against Chicago, logging a 2.81 ERA with 29 strikeouts and five walks in 25 2/3 innings over four starts.
If you like pitchers with overpowering stuff, Game 2 could be appointment viewing. This season, Williams racked up 248 strikeouts (second in MLB to Jacob Misiorowski’s 252) in 184 1/3 innings over 32 starts, all of which were career highs. He had double-digit punchouts in 11 of those outings, which led the Majors.
None of those 11 starts were against Chicago, though Williams did record a 3.98 ERA with 28 strikeouts and eight walks in 20 1/3 innings over four starts against the White Sox. His Game 2 assignment is noteworthy because it lines him up to pitch Game 5 (if necessary) back in Cleveland, whereas Messick is lined up for Game 4 in Chicago. Williams had a 2.84 ERA in 18 home starts this season, and a 5.05 ERA in 14 road starts.
The Guardians are still working through their plan here. Manager Stephen Vogt noted Thursday that they want to see how Games 1 and 2 go and what their potential needs are before making a decision.
Why could it be Espino? Of the 14 position players on the White Sox Wild Card Series roster, there were six lefties and one switch-hitter. Starting Espino as an opener for lefty Joey Cantillo could force Chicago to make a lineup decision, such as whether to start lefty smasher Randal Grichuk against Espino, or call his number after Cantillo enters.
Espino served as an opener in Cantillo’s final three appearances of the regular season after the lefty encountered some command issues. Cantillo tossed 15 scoreless innings, allowing five hits and four walks, while striking out 17 batters in those outings. The formula could work in October.
All that being said: The Guardians have a flurry of options, between Espino/Cantillo, Tanner Bibee and Foster Griffin. Stay tuned.
White Sox
Some of the TBDs in terms of White Sox starters were cleared up on Friday by manager Will Venable. It begins with Smith, the rookie southpaw, who gets the same Game 1 honor as he did in the sweep of Houston during the AL Wild Card Series.
“They're a really good team. This will be my third time playing [them] since I got up here,” Smith said Friday. “So just kind of familiar with the guys and their lineup and familiar with the scouting reports against them. We are both good teams. We play hard. They play hard. So it's going to be a good series.“
With Sunday’s off-day, Burke would be pitching on regular rest Monday after striking out eight over four innings against the Astros on Wednesday. Venable confirmed Friday that Burke will pitch on Monday and will not pitch on Saturday, but the skipper did not confirm if it would be as a starter or bulk hurler.
Burke recently joked that the White Sox have 13 pitchers, or 12 in the Wild Card round, but they don’t look at anyone as a starter or reliever. This is not a situation of trying to outsmart the opposition by usage of an opener, but it’s more about Venable and his staff trying to win each game and nothing more. It has produced one of the best Major League Baseball stories this season, so why change now?
Again, Kay would make sense, having last pitched Wednesday. But he might be needed in one of the first two games. Everything is fluid.
One thing to consider: Davis Martin has a 5-3 record with a 3.13 ERA over 15 home starts against a 4-5 record and 4.68 ERA over 14 appearances (13 starts) on the road. Let’s not forget rookie Noah Schultz, who has been impressive working multiple innings out of the bullpen, or rookie David Sandlin, a starter who worked in relief against the Astros. Sean Newcomb has done a little bit of everything this season, with a 3.24 ERA over eight games against the Guardians. So he’s always a possibility.
Don’t overlook Smith coming back, with Venable discussing Smith and Taylor potentially being available for all three games.

item.content:encoded:
Braves' Walt Weiss provides update on Chris Sale NLDS plan appeared first on ClutchPoints. Add ClutchPoints as a Preferred Source by clicking here.
The Atlanta Braves have been meticulous in how they handle Chris Sale for the last three years, making sure to give him enough rest so that he can maintain his excellent form for an entire campaign. The 2024 National League Cy Young Award winner has still spent time on the injured list, but their plan has helped him become a top-tier starting pitcher once again. All bets are off in the playoffs, though. Right?
Two days after starting Game 1 of the NL Wild Card Series versus the Philadelphia Phillies, Sale made it clear he wanted to take the mound in a do-or-die Game 3. Despite holding a 6-2 lead in the eighth inning, manager Walt Weiss brought in the veteran left-hander to finish off Atlanta's longtime rival. Sale indicated that he still plans to pitch against the Los Angeles Dodgers on Sunday night, but nothing is official yet.
In fact, it sounds like there is serious doubt surrounding the 10-time All-Star's status for Game 2 of the NL Division Series. Although Weiss said a Sale start in LA is "still on the table," the Braves want their ace to be fresh enough for postseason battle.
Watch sports LIVE with fuboTV (free trial)
"We're gonna err on the side of giving him (time to rest) if it's even close," the NL Manager of the Year candidate revealed, per ESPN's Alden Gonzalez. That statement is a far cry from Sale's confident remarks following Atlanta's series-clinching win over Philly. Weiss has been in baseball a long time, however.
It is possible the skipper is just engaging in some good old-fashioned gamesmanship before his squad faces the two-time reigning World Series champions. The Braves are a title contender in their own right, but they will want to gain a mental edge on the Dodgers if one is attainable. Disarming the home team with a surprise pitching move seems like the perfect gambit to try in October. Dave Roberts is a veteran of this game as well, though, so he may not be caught off guard.
Of course, there is a possibility that Walt Weiss is merely telling the truth. Perhaps Atlanta will wait until it returns to Truist Park to start Chris Sale. If so, then the team's bullpen move in Game 3 of the Wild Card round will seem even more puzzling.
One thing is for certain. Sale is a warrior who has openly expressed his desire to carry a big workload in the playoffs. We shall see if the Braves trust him to run wild in Chavez Ravine. The time for speculation will soon end. Game 1 of the NLDS begins on Saturday at 4 p.m. ET.

"I think this year is the bigge
item.content:encoded:
Phillies fans responded to shortstop Trea Turner's comments about his offensive performance during the postgame interview following Philadelphia's early postseason exit on Thursday. The Phillies lost the deciding game of the NLWCS to the Braves on Thursday, failing to advance to the NLDS.
In an interview clip shared by NBC Philadelphia's John Clark, Turner admitted to a poor season at the plate and said he had to find answers to his struggles during the offseason. "I think this year is the biggest question mark for me offensively in a long time. I've got a lot of work to do," Turner said about his 2026 offensive woes.
Watch the video here:
Philadelphia fans were quick to notice Turner's comments in the postgame interview. They slammed the shortstop for his hesitant response to the question, sharing their blunt reactions on social media.
"300 mil of work to do. Go to another team, thanks," one fan commented.
Many fans fired shots at Turner by recalling his massive 11-year, $300 million contract, which he signed with the team during the 2022 offseason. The contract officially runs until 2033, and that has made multiple fans concerned about his form at the plate in the past few years.
Trea Turner Produced Disappointing Numbers at the Plate in 2026
Overall, Turner finished the regular season with a .242 batting average, 19 home runs, 58 RBIs, and a .675 OPS. These numbers are comparable to those from his rookie season with the Washington Nationals in 2015.
The Phillies invested heavily in the shortstop, who has a strong track record on both offense and defense. However, he has not yet realized his full potential for the team and its dedicated fans.
In the three NLWCS games against Atlanta, Turner managed only one hit, scoring one run and recording one RBI, stats that fall short of expectations for a star slugger in such important playoff matchups.
However, the three-time All-Star and 2019 World Series champion now has a lot to figure out during the offseason to come back stronger next year.

item.title: [Yahoo Sports] Dodgers postseason primer: Where do Shohei Ohtani and everyone else stand as they go for a three-peat?
item.dc:creator: Jack Baer

item.content:encoded:
The Los Angeles Dodgers' quest for a three-peat begins in earnest on Saturday with Game 1 of the NLDS, as they seek to become the first time since the 1998-2000 New York Yankees to complete a trilogy of titles.
Up to this point, the path for L.A. hasn't been entirely straightforward. There have been times when the Dodgers have looked a bit rickety, and that's to say nothing about everything happening off the field. They are also arguably the most talented team in the playoffs and are coming off another 100-win season.
No matter how you slice it, this is a club with more than its fair share of questions. Let's get into them, starting with the easier ones.
Who are the Dodgers playing in the NLDS?
The Dodgers will face the NL East champion Atlanta Braves, who defeated the Philadelphia Phillies in a three-game wild-card series. The Dodgers went 1-5 against Atlanta in the regular season, getting outscored 26-15.
The winner of the best-of-five series gets the victor of the other NLDS between the Milwaukee Brewers and San Diego Padres.
When do the Dodgers play?
Here's the full NLDS schedule:
| Game | Date | Time (ET) | Channel | Location |
| 1 | Oct. 3 | 4 p.m. | Fox | L.A. |
| 2 | Oct. 4 | 8 p.m. | FS1 | L.A. |
| 3 | Oct. 6 | 6 p.m. | FS1 | Atlanta |
| 4* | Oct. 7 | 6 p.m. | FS1 | Atlanta |
| 5* | Oct. 9 | 8 p.m. | Fox | L.A. |
*if necessary
What will the Dodgers' postseason lineup be?
The Dodgers finished the season shuffling their lineup depending on the handedness of the opposing starting pitcher, and it stands to reason that they will continue doing so in the postseason.
Here's how they could line up against right-handed pitchers:
- Shohei Ohtani, DH
- Mookie Betts, SS
- Freddie Freeman, 1B
- Will Smith, C
- Kyle Tucker, RF
- Teoscar Hernández, LF
- Max Muncy, 3B
- Andy Pages, CF
- Tommy Edman, 2B
Shohei Ohtani has never hit in a batting order position other than leadoff in his MLB postseason career, but lately he has been hitting second against left-handers while Mookie Betts takes his old position atop the order.
Here's L.A.'s left-handed unit:
- Mookie Betts, SS
- Shohei Ohtani, DH
- Freddie Freeman, 1B
- Will Smith, C
- Teoscar Hernández, LF
- Kyle Tucker, RF
- Andy Pages, CF
- Max Muncy, 3B
- Tommy Edman, 2B
Both of those orders alternate left-right all the way down to Edman, a switch-hitter at the bottom. It's entirely possible the Dodgers go a different route, too.
What will the Dodgers' postseason rotation be?
That's fairly settled. The Dodgers will trot out the quartet of Yoshinobu Yamamoto, Tarik Skubal, Blake Snell and Tyler Glasnow. The order in which those arms are utilized remains to be seen, though the Dodgers have every reason to maximize innings for Yamamoto after what he did last year.
How has this season gone for the Dodgers?
It has gone well, by the standards of any other team.
By the standards of the Dodgers, well, there are a few dynamics at play. This is a good baseball team. They probably should've been better this season, and not just because they have the largest payroll in history, at a projected $410 million, per Roster Resource.
A two-time World Series champion filled its two biggest roster holes by giving two players, Kyle Tucker and Edwin Díaz, the highest salaries in the history of their positions. Entering the season, the Dodgers were estimated by the usually conservative PECOTA projections from Baseball Prospectus to win 104 games, and that didn't take into account acquiring a two-time reigning Cy Young Award winner in Skubal and more at the MLB trade deadline.
So in that sense, 100 wins is a disappointment. One of the most talented teams in MLB history (on paper at least) had more than its fair share of injuries, underperformances and mistakes. There was a point when the club seemed on the verge of letting the NL West become a race, as the Arizona Diamondbacks halved a division lead from 14 games to seven in the span of about a month between July and August, but then the D-backs got mired in their own slump and the Dodgers got hot again.
Overall, the Dodgers' issues boiled down to an offense that slumped hard in July and August, rough days for starting pitchers who will not be starting games in the playoffs and an epically bad bullpen night here and there. The first of those got better in September, though, which you can read more about here.
There is also the Dodgers' 38-37 record against teams with winning records this season, as their worst stretches of the year coincided with some of their toughest road trips and homestands, and that can leave an impression. Of course, it's a bit silly to worry about a team handling its business against good teams when it's going for a three-peat.
How does this team compare to last year's?
It's easy to remember the 2024 and 2025 Dodgers as juggernauts, but both of those teams had flaws that easily could've been fatal.
The 2024 Dodgers entered the postseason with a three-man rotation of Yamamoto, Walker Buehler and Jack Flaherty, with Clayton Kershaw, Glasnow, Dustin May, Gavin Stone, River Ryan and Emmet Sheehan among the starting pitchers on the injured list.
That team was so desperate for starting pitching help that it went full bullpen game while facing elimination at the hands of the Padres in the NLDS. It was only through the grace of a deep and competent bullpen that L.A. triumphed.
The 2025 team had the opposite problem. No one was doubting a rotation of Yamamoto, Snell, Glasnow and Ohtani, but there were most certainly concerns about a bullpen whose late-inning arms consistently blew games well into September.
Once again, the Dodgers adjusted. With their rotation overflowing, they turned to a number of starting pitchers to fill the gaps. Every single pitcher who appeared in Game 7 of the 2025 World Series started at least nine games for this year's team.
With that in mind, the 2026 Dodgers might be the franchise's most balanced roster to enter the postseason in years, but there is once again a major question.
It's Ohtani. Let's get into that.
How's Shohei Ohtani doing?
Ohtani was the overwhelming NL MVP front-runner for the first half of this season, having begun the year as both a hitter and a pitcher for the first time in his Dodgers career.
Then Ohtani's knee started barking in July, resulting in the team taking him off the mound and giving him a lubricant injection during the All-Star break. He also developed a biceps issue at some point.
Those injuries didn't immediately stop Ohtani from playing. Much like he did in his recovery from internal brace surgery in 2024 and 2025, Ohtani played as the Dodgers' every-day designated hitter while rehabbing. However, the injuries clearly started to affect him in September, and the Dodgers opted to put him on the injured list for the first time in his tenure with the team.
Ohtani returned with five games left in the regular season and went 5-for-21 with 1 walk, 8 strikeouts and one extra-base hit, a double. Those numbers clearly aren't up to his standards, but if there's a reason for optimism, it's that he hit batted balls with exit velocities of 106.8, 106, 103.9 and 103.4 mph. He hadn't hit a ball that hard since August. Of course, the flip side of that optimism is maybe a 100% version of him would've hit them even harder.
Since his return, the Dodgers have insisted that Ohtani is feeling better, with hitting coach Aaron Bates saying Thursday that they had absolutely no concerns. The ship has sailed on Ohtani pitching again this season, though.
It still feels like Ohtani is the single biggest question for the Dodgers entering this postseason, given how long-term his knee issue has been. He at least got plenty of rest between his 15-day IL stint and the five days off between the end of the regular season and the start of the NLDS.
Do the Dodgers have a young, dynamic replacement at DH if Ohtani isn't healthy?
What an oddly specific question. The answer is yes, potentially.
It's not a stretch to say that Josue De Paula was the best hitting prospect in baseball at the time of his promotion to fill Ohtani's roster spot in September. At the time, every other position player in the MLB Pipeline top 10 was a shortstop who could offer significant two-way value, while De Paula will eventually be a bat-first corner outfielder at best and a bat-only first baseman at worst.
The good news is De Paula definitely looked like he belonged in his 11 games with the Dodgers while Ohtani was on the IL, slashing .323/.500/.581 and helping inject life into a previously struggling lineup. He was optioned when Ohtani came back, the timing of which made him available for the start of the NLDS.
In the playoffs, De Paula is likely to be the Dodgers' top left-handed bat off the bench, and he could fit in at designated hitter or corner outfield if someone gets hurt. It seems highly unlikely, however, that the Dodgers will take any plate appearances from Ohtani, barring a significant aggravation of that knee issue.
Are Kyle Tucker and Edwin Díaz still having horrifically bad debut seasons for the Dodgers?
Those two players were the butt of jokes all season after they signed record contracts to join the defending champions, then posted the worst seasons of their careers. However, both offered reason for optimism in September.
Tucker entered the month slashing .228/.326/.357 but finished the season at .262/.354/.536, numbers more in line with what the Dodgers were expecting when they signed him to a four-year, $240 million contract. His six homers in September were double what he had in any other month of the season.
In 2026, Díaz made seven appearances with a 10.50 ERA, spent three months on the injured list due to loose bodies in his elbow, came back for nine more appearances, posted a 12.91 ERA in those, then hit the IL one more time in August due to what was described as neck inflammation.
Then he came back in September and, like Tucker, performed like the player the Dodgers were initially expecting, with nine strikeouts and one hit allowed across five scoreless innings. Díaz no longer has the closer role, but he made as good a case as he could for late-inning work in October.
Tucker and Díaz still finished the year with horrendous numbers, and barring some postseason heroics, that's what most fans will remember. Still, it's important to know that the Dodgers might not treat them in October like their overall numbers would suggest.
How's the rest of the Dodgers' bullpen shaping up?
It's a diverse group. We've already talked about Díaz, who could be anything from middle reliever to closer by the end of the postseason. However, the current closer is Tanner Scott, who played the Díaz role last year as the high-priced reliever who struggled in his first year with the Dodgers.
Scott's second season in L.A. has gone far better. He converted 25 of 29 save attempts with a 2.69 ERA.
As for the other six spots in the bullpen, the contenders are Edgardo Henriquez, Alex Vesia, Evan Phillips, Kris Bubic and Brock Stewart from the normal pot of relievers and Roki Sasaki, Justin Wrobleski and Sheehan as overflow from the rotation.
Henriquez might be the most intriguing name from that group, as the flame-throwing right-hander was great during the regular season, only to hit the IL due to lower back discomfort in September. The Dodgers think he's trending toward playing in the NLDS.
Does a Dodgers World Series guarantee a salary cap?
You'd think. Some certainly seem to think. However, let's take a view rooted not in optimism but in realism.
The owners want a salary cap. They wanted one before Shohei Ohtani signed on the dotted line of a $700 million contract. They wanted one before Shohei Ohtani was born (what else happened in 1994?). They want a salary cap for the same reason every owner in sports has wanted a salary cap — not for competitive balance but to remove pressure on them to spend like they want to compete.
The Dodgers have made for a convenient boogeyman by being baseball's biggest spender and baseball's best team over the past several years. They must be stopped to save baseball, or so the argument goes, as no team is supposed to have L.A.'s combination of resources, competence and aggression. It's just not fair. It almost goes without saying in many discussions that the point of a salary cap is to end the Dodgers' unfair dynasty.
And yet, it really needs to be noted: Commissioner Rob Manfred does not fantasize about the Dodgers being forced to dismantle their tremendous machine — of Andrew Friedman, on his knees, begging a small-market team to take Glasnow's contract off his books — like some salary-cap proponents seem to do. Ohtani winning rings on the Dodgers has worked out quite nicely for baseball. A salary cap can be introduced for cost control and the veneer of parity, but MLB ultimately benefits from the large-market teams being contenders with the biggest stars. As such, it's hard to imagine a salary cap being introduced in such a way that the Dodgers, Yankees, Mets and other top spenders are forced to take immediate action to get below a line. A slow introduction of a cap or some sort of contract grandfathering seems far more likely, giving the Dodgers and others time to adjust.
The Dodgers' recent success isn't so much fuel for a salary cap as it is fuel for salary-cap opinions. It has certainly convinced many fans of a salary cap's necessity, but the MLBPA is playing cards at a different table. They don't want a salary cap, no matter what the Dodgers do, and they and the MLB owners are ultimately the people whose opinions matter here.
Limitations on the Dodgers would merely be a byproduct of MLB getting what it wants, and that would be completely antithetical to the history of the union. It's difficult to imagine the next month impacting salary-cap discussions to any significant degree.
What about the money problems with Dodgers ownership?
That's still in progress, and it remains unclear how much it will affect the Dodgers.
The short version of a very complicated story is that the companies operated by Dodgers majority owner Mark Walter were found to be doing business with one another at a rate much greater than what they were telling customers, investors and regulators. Walter is now facing considerable legal scrutiny and has reacted by selling whatever he can to pay off some of the loans that turned out to be less than kosher.
His biggest move was to sell his majority stake in the Los Angeles Lakers at a franchise valuation of $12.5 billion, one year after buying the team at a $10 billion valuation. He has also offloaded his stake in the Premier League club Chelsea and the Ligue 1 club Strasbourg.
Those were big parts of Walter's sports portfolio, which also includes the WNBA's Los Angeles Sparks, the Cadillac Formula 1 team, the entire Professional Women's Hockey League and, of course, the Dodgers.
Dodgers leadership has repeatedly said the team isn't for sale. Of course, any sale would probably come out of nowhere — the Lakers' move was dropped on an otherwise uneventful Wednesday morning — but for now, that's mere speculation with the Dodgers.
One notable sign of trouble in Chavez Ravine, though, was a report that Walter recently approached Charter Communications about letting them out of their famously expensive Dodgers (and Lakers) contracts in exchange for a lump sum payout. It appears nothing has come out of that, but those are not stories you hear when everything is going well.
All of that's to say that Walter would likely welcome the immediate financial benefit of winning a third straight World Series even more than your typical billionaire. Of course, that outcome isn't up to him.

item.title: [Sportsnaut] Phillies Could Trade Kyle Schwarber This Winter? 5 Potential Destinations After New Speculation, Including the NY Yankees
item.dc:creator: Jasonburgosmma; Jason Burgos
item.description: After a disappointing end to the 2026 season, a notable MLB insider believes the Philadelphia Phillies will consider trading star slugger Kyle Schwarber this winter. The Phillies entered this year with the fourth-highest payroll in MLB and big expectations. While they didn’t win the National League East, the hope was that their talent-rich roster could still go on a deep run in the postseason. Unfortunately, despite their best efforts, Philadelphia came up short in their three-game Wild Card ser
item.content:encoded:
After a disappointing end to the 2026 season, a notable MLB insider believes the Philadelphia Phillies will consider trading star slugger Kyle Schwarber this winter.
The Phillies entered this year with the fourth-highest payroll in MLB and big expectations. While they didn’t win the National League East, the hope was that their talent-rich roster could still go on a deep run in the postseason. Unfortunately, despite their best efforts, Philadelphia came up short in their three-game Wild Card series against division rivals the Atlanta Braves.
Following their season-ending loss on Thursday, The Athletic’s Ken Rosenthal claimed, “The Phillies at least need to kick around the idea of trading” the All-Star DH. A player the MLB insider feels doesn’t have an “oppressive” contract with four years and $120 million left on the deal.
While it is likely Schwarber is playing for the Phillies in 2027 and beyond, especially since he has a full no-trade clause, if the team did look to trade him this winter, here are five teams he could end up going to in the offseason.
Detroit Tigers
After trading top star Tarik Skubal before this season’s trade deadline, the Detroit Tigers will probably be open to diverting the money they were willing to give the reigning American League Cy Young to a different star.
While the Tigers are in greater need of elite pitching, adding one of the best sluggers in the game would be a massive addition for their lineup in 2027. Furthermore, after trading the two-time All-Star ace in the summer, they certainly now have the prospect assets that would interest the Phillies.
Toronto Blue Jays
This season was a massive disappointment for the Toronto Blue Jays. After being a couple of outs away from winning the World Series last fall, the Jays finished dead last in the AL East with a 79-83 record this year. So you can bet they will look to make a big move this offseason to get back into title contention in 2027.
If the Phillies actually make Schwarber available in trade talks, Toronto will be fascinated by the idea of pairing him with Vladimir Guerrero Jr. next season. The idea of Schwarber and Guerrero Jr. in the same batting order will give other AL East pitching staffs a cold sweat.
New York Yankees
The New York Yankees are still in the race to be champions in 2026. However, if they fall short of that yearly goal, the Yanks will surely look into adding a piece or two that can get them to end their 17-year title drought.
New York would need to find a new home for Giancarlo Stanton, but with only one guaranteed season for $15 million left on his deal, it may be possible this offseason. If they can trade the injury-prone five-time All-Star, Aaron Judge and Schwarber in the same lineup would be the most terrifying back-to-back in baseball.
Cincinnati Reds
To the surprise of many, the Cincinnati Reds were serious about bringing Schwarber back to his native Ohio this past offseason. And the 33-year-old was allegedly open to the idea as well. However, the draw of playing for a title contender he was familiar with and a huge contract brought him back to Philadelphia. The Reds would have some solid youngsters to offer in a trade, including top prospects that got the call to the big leagues this year.
Boston Red Sox
After a disappointing performance in the playoffs, it would not be a surprise if the Boston Red Sox looked to make a major move or two this winter. They don’t have an obvious DH for next season, so Schwarber would fill a clear need. Furthermore, slotting him into the middle of their batting order would make life far easier and offer more opportunities for Roman Anthony, Willson Contreras, and Adley Rutschman to drive in runs.

item.dc:creator: Global Sports Desk

item.content:encoded:
While Francisco Lindor’s baseball career has made him one of the most recognizable players on the New York Mets, his life away from the diamond has become an equally important part of his public story. Puerto Rican shortstop reached another career milestone on September 27, 2026, hitting his 300th career home run against the Washington Nationals. The feat also made him just the 11th switch-hitter in MLB history to reach the 300 home run mark, and the second, behind Carlos Beltran, to combine that feat with at least 200 stolen bases.
Off the field, Lindor is married to his wife, Katia Reguero. The couple are proud parents of three children. The couple met on Instagram in 2020, before marrying in December 2021, and now share children Kalina Zoé, 3, and Amapola Chloé, 2, and son Koa Amani, 1. Reguero has also developed her own public persona through music, parenting talks and community work.
Francisco Lindor and Katia Reguero’s family life beyond Mets stardom
Francisco Lindor and Katia Reguero have raised a family and juggled the demanding schedule that comes with Major League Baseball. Lindor’s career involves plenty of travel, a long regular season and public scrutiny at all times, while Reguero has built her own professional and creative interests.
The couple have three children, Kalina Zoé born in November 2020, Amapola Chloé born in June 2023, and Koa Amani born in March 2025. Koa was born in the middle of the MLB season, and Lindor returned to the New York Mets shortly after his son’s birth. MLB said the Mets were preparing to play the Miami Marlins the following day, and Lindor was with the team.
Francisco Lindor and Katia Reguero’s marriage and children
Francisco Lindor and Katia Reguero's relationship began online in early 2020. Lindor messaged Reguero on Instagram, and they talked for about three months before meeting in person in Arizona. They ended up getting married, and their relationship blossomed as Lindor continued his baseball career.
The couple said "I do" on December 16, 2021, at Vizcaya Museum and Gardens in Miami, Florida. Their marriage came after they already had Kalina, giving the family a personal foundation before their wedding.
As Lindor’s career has progressed, so have family milestones. Lindor went back to be with Reguero when Koa was born in March 2025 and returned to the Mets. The moment illustrated how a player at the highest level can have family obligations and a demanding baseball schedule intersect.
Francisco Lindor and Katia Reguero’s lives beyond baseball
Lindor is more than his stats and his accomplishments with the New York Mets. His work with youth clinics, Boys & Girls Clubs and the Lindor Smiles community initiative is noted in MLB’s official profile, as well as a scholarship fund he created at Montverde Academy and a $1 million donation to the school’s Lindor Hall project.
Katia Reguero has also kept up interests outside of being Lindor’s wife. She has a background in music and has become known for her podcast and advocacy work in parenting. She also got noticed in 2026 playing the national anthem on violin at a New York Mets game, bringing another facet of her identity into the baseball environment around her family.
In September 2026, Lindor hit his 300th career home run, another milestone in his baseball career. Off the field, though, his life is one of marriage, three children, involvement in the community, and a wife who has built a public career in her own right. All of those factors combine to give a broader picture of the New York Mets star than just being an MLB shortstop.

item.title: [Yahoo Sports] Dodgers rotation is their greatest strength this October
item.dc:creator: Eric Stephen
item.description: LOS ANGELES — The Dodgers won a championship in 2024 with a decimated starting rotation and dominant bullpen, then flipped the script with a stellar rotation buoying a shaky bullpen to win another title in 2025. This year the Dodgers might have melded the two heading into October. "We have a lot of really talented arms," general manager Brandon Gomes said Tuesday. "I think this is about as deep of a pitching staff as we've ever had. There's a lot of really good options to work through as a group
item.content:encoded:
LOS ANGELES — The Dodgers won a championship in 2024 with a decimated starting rotation and dominant bullpen, then flipped the script with a stellar rotation buoying a shaky bullpen to win another title in 2025. This year the Dodgers might have melded the two heading into October.
"We have a lot of really talented arms," general manager Brandon Gomes said Tuesday. "I think this is about as deep of a pitching staff as we've ever had. There's a lot of really good options to work through as a group."
For now, we'll focus on the rotation, which looks just as strong this year as it did last October, even though Shohei Ohtani hasn't pitched since July 3 and will not pitch this postseason. The Dodgers filled that slot with a two-time Cy Young Award winner, trading for Tarik Skubal on August 2.
Yoshinobu Yamamoto was again the rock of the starting rotation, making every start for the second year in a row. Blake Snell and Tyler Glasnow each missed multiple months with a long injured-list stint in season, then returned with enough of a runway to get ready for October. All four put up solid numbers this season.
| Pitcher | Starts | IP | ERA | xERA | BB rate | K rate |
| Skubal | 26 | 158.7 | 2.72 | 2.94 | 4.4% | 30.0% |
| Yamamoto | 28 | 185 | 2.53 | 2.94 | 5.9% | 25.7% |
| Snell | 9 | 62 | 1.90 | 2.17 | 9.2% | 31.8% |
| Glasnow | 13 | 74 | 3.53 | 2.86 | 8.7% | 34.0% |
*Skubal's numbers include Tigers & Dodgers
"To be honest, we can kind of really put all four guys in a hat, and run them out there," manager Dave Roberts said Tuesday.
Last year, Yamamoto, Snell, Ohtani, and Glasnow combined to start all 17 postseason games, and put up a collective 2.55 ERA in 113 innings, with 127 strikeouts and a 28.5-percent strikeout rate. All four of them pitched in Game 7 of the World Series, including Yamamoto getting the final eight outs one day after winning Game 6 as the starter. Yamamoto last October pitched the Dodgers' first two postseason compete games since 1988, and Blake Snell had starts of eight and seven innings as well.
Quality starts are a bit crude, but criticism tends to focus on the minimum requirements — at least six innings, with no more than three earned runs allowed. But across MLB this regular season, teams went 1,094-484 (.693) in games when they got a quality start, with a collective 1.74 ERA from the starters in those games.
This season, the Dodgers led the majors with 83 quality starts, eight more than the next-best team, the Philadelphia Phillies. Those 83 quality starts by the Dodgers this year were their most since 2015, when they got 95 quality starts from a rotation that included the second- and third-place finishers in National League Cy Young Award voting (Zack Greinke, Clayton Kershaw). They were 60-23 (.723) when getting a quality start in 2026.
Dodgers starters last postseason had 10 quality starts, more than any pitching staff since the 2013 Detroit Tigers. Those 10 quality starts in 17 games were one more than the Dodgers had in their previous five postseasons combined, totaling 53 games.
Last postseason, the Dodgers won all 10 of the games in which they received a quality start, with zero or one run allowed by the starter in seven of those games. Two of those quality starts were by Ohtani, but he's replaced in the rotation by Skubal, who last postseason posted three quality starts in his three tries, totaling 36 strikeouts and four runs allowed in his 20 2/3 innings for the Detroit Tigers.
"Watching Tarik Skubal pitch in the playoffs last year was must-see TV. I was in awe, watching the energy, the dominance he exhibited there," Dodgers president of baseball operations Andrew Friedman said in August after trading for Skubal. "I can't wait to see it on our club."

item.title: [Bleacher Report] Tarik Skubal's New Landing Spots Predicted by Insiders Ahead of MLB Free Agency
item.dc:creator: Adam Wells

In a survey of MLB insiders conducted by ESPN's Kiley McDaniel, the Dodgers, New York Mets and Detroit Tigers were cited as the "true contenders" for the two-time AL Cy Young winner. The New York Yankees were cited as being "just behin
item.content:encoded:
Tarik Skubal's New Landing Spots Predicted by Insiders Ahead of MLB Free Agency
As Tarik Skubal prepares for his first postseason with the Los Angeles Dodgers, people within MLB are also looking ahead to his free agency and which team he might end up signing with.
In a survey of MLB insiders conducted by ESPN's Kiley McDaniel, the Dodgers, New York Mets and Detroit Tigers were cited as the "true contenders" for the two-time AL Cy Young winner.
The New York Yankees were cited as being "just behind" the lead group in how often they were mentioned.
In the group of sleepers, McDaniel listed the Chicago White Sox, San Diego Padres and Los Angeles Angels as teams that frequently came up.
The Tigers, who traded Skubal to Los Angeles on Aug. 2, are the most interesting of the top group because they don't usually play in the deep end of the free-agent pool.
If they were going to sign Skubal, the Tigers could have just done it last offseason to avoid reaching the point where they had to trade him. He told USA Today's Bob Nightengale during spring training there was "no offer" that came from Detroit.
The Dodgers aren't a surprise given Skubal is already there and they have a habit of signing the best free agent every year, but McDaniel did note the respondents had "some hesitation" about including them given the uncertainty around their ownership situation with Mark Walter at the moment.
Even though Walter sold his majority stake in the Los Angeles Lakers earlier this year just 10 months after his purchase was finalized, Dodgers officials have strongly maintained the MLB club is not being sold.
It will be interesting to see how aggressive the Mets want to be this offseason after a 74-88 record in 2026. They spent almost $240 million in free agency last winter, but fans were unhappy about the ways they invested their money.
Mets president of baseball operations David Stearns could also be feeling a lot of pressure given that he was at the center of a lot of vitriol from fans in Queens for things like not even attempting to bring back Pete Alonso before he signed with the Baltimore Orioles.
Among the three sleeper teams listed by McDaniel, the White Sox stand out as a team that could make a huge leap to being a top-tier AL team if they upgrade their rotation. The offense ranked fifth in runs scored and sixth in homers this season.
The Angels are in a fascinating position because Stan Kroenke is set to take over as owner after agreeing to buy the club from Arte Moreno for $3.9 billion.
Kroenke's purchase still has to be approved and the timing of that could impact how aggressive they are in free agency, but it's not uncommon for a new ownership team to want to make an aggressive splash right out of the gate.
The downside, though, is the Angels are so far away from being a contender after losing a franchise-record 100 games with a middling farm system, albeit one that is improving, that giving a huge sum of money to Skubal right now may not be the best team-building strategy even if it would make them more interesting in the short-term.
Skubal finished the 2026 regular season with a 2.72 ERA and 186 strikeouts in 158.2 innings over 26 starts between the Tigers and Dodgers. This was his fourth consecutive season with a sub-3.00 ERA and at least 10.0 strikeouts per nine innings.

item.title: [New York Post] Dodgers to tab new ace in surprise Game 1 playoff rotation decision
item.dc:creator: Jack Harris
item.description: To begin their quest for a third-straight World Series this postseason, the Dodgers will turn to the one pitcher in their rotation yet to win a championship ring. Tarik Skubal is expected to be named the team’s starter for Game 1 of the National League Division Series against the Atlanta Braves on Saturday, a source with knowledge of the situation told the California Post, giving the reigning two-time Cy Young Award winner and marquee trade deadline acquisition an immediate opportunity to jump-s
item.content:encoded:
To begin their quest for a third-straight World Series this postseason, the Dodgers will turn to the one pitcher in their rotation yet to win a championship ring.
Tarik Skubal is expected to be named the team’s starter for Game 1 of the National League Division Series against the Atlanta Braves on Saturday, a source with knowledge of the situation told the California Post, giving the reigning two-time Cy Young Award winner and marquee trade deadline acquisition an immediate opportunity to jump-start the club’s three-peat bid.
The Dodgers, of course, had no bad options for their playoff opener.
Their rotation includes four pitchers who would be No. 1 options on most other clubs, with Skubal being joined by Yoshinobu Yamamoto, Blake Snell and Tyler Glasnow for this year’s October push.
However, Skubal is set to get the nod, as The Athletic first reported, after increasingly impressive late-season performances with the Dodgers following his blockbuster arrival from the Detroit Tigers in August.
The 29-year-old left-hander posted a 5-2 record and 2.61 ERA in 10 post-deadline starts with the club, improving upon the 7-5 mark and 2.79 ERA he had with the Tigers during a first half that was sidetracked by an elbow procedure that sidelined him for all of May.
Skubal’s best outings came in the final weeks of the regular season, when he spun a pair of scoreless seven-inning starts in two of his final three appearances of the campaign.
Prior to Friday’s news, there was a thought that Yamamoto would be the Dodgers’ Game 1 starter, given his World Series MVP heroics last fall.
But Yamamoto threw extensively in a simulated game on Wednesday, during the club’s bye week workouts. That kept him on his customary once-per-week pitching schedule (his regular-season finale came on the Wednesday before that) and might line him up to pitch in Game 3 in Atlanta next Tuesday instead. Of note: Yamamoto has notably better splits on the road (1.77 ERA) than at home (3.13 ERA) this year.
Snell, who has followed Skubal in the Dodgers’ rotation lately, seems like the logical candidate to start Game 2 on Sunday. Glasnow, who pitched in another simulated game Thursday, figures to go in Game 4, and could be an option out of the bullpen this weekend.
While Skubal –– who will be the sport’s top free agent this winter –– has yet to win a World Series, he does have a sterling postseason track record.
In six playoff outings over the last two years with the Tigers, he pitched to a 2.04 ERA while striking out 56 batters in 39 ⅔ innings. Those numbers would be even better if not for his one October clunker, when he gave up five runs in a winner-take-all loss in Game 5 of the 2024 American League Division Series.
That failure has become a motivator for Skubal in the two years since. It has left him with a feeling of unfinished business as he begins another playoff campaign amid new surroundings now.
“Once the months change and the playoffs start, nothing matters,” he said last week. “It’s just about winning that game, and that’s how I treat every single start. Because I’m just trying to put our team in a position to win a baseball game. That won’t change from today, and whenever my next start is.”

item.content:encoded:
Published Oct 2, 2026 10:17 am
NEW YORK (AP) — Chicago Cubs center fielder Pete Crow-Armstrong won the Baseball Digest major league player of the year award Friday, and Milwaukee Brewers ace Jacob Misiorowski was selected pitcher of the year.
San Diego Padres closer Mason Miller was chosen reliever of the year.
Crow-Armstrong batted .280 with 45 home runs and 41 stolen bases this season, becoming the seventh member of the 40-40 club.
He led the majors in runs (119), tied for most homers, ranked second in OPS (.943) and finished fourth in RBIs (107). All while playing outstanding defense and appearing in all 162 regular-season games to help the Cubs earn a National League wild card.
The 24-year-old Crow-Armstrong received 21 of 24 first-place votes in balloting by a panel of baseball writers, broadcasters, reporters and researchers that included several former players, managers and executives.
Houston Astros slugger Yordan Alvarez finished second.
Crow-Armstrong became the seventh Cubs player to win the Baseball Digest award and first since Kris Bryant and Anthony Rizzo shared the prize in 2016.
The hard-throwing Misiorowski also garnered 21 first-place votes after going 16-5 to propel Milwaukee to the best record in the big leagues (103-59) and its fourth consecutive NL Central title. He led the majors with a 1.80 ERA and 252 strikeouts in 30 starts covering 174 2/3 innings.
New York Yankees right-hander Cam Schlittler was runner-up to the 24-year-old Misiorowski, the first Brewers pitcher to take home the honor.
Miller, 28, tied for the NL lead with a career-high 38 saves as the Padres earned a wild-card spot in the playoffs. He went 5-2 with a 1.67 ERA and 129 strikeouts in 70 innings over 66 appearances.
The right-hander received 18 first-place votes and easily outpaced Cleveland Guardians closer Cade Smith, who came in second.
___

item.content:encoded:
Cubs' Pete Crow-Armstrong makes honest admission about struggles in NL Wild Card against Padres originally appeared on The Sporting News. Add The Sporting News as a Preferred Source by clicking here.
It was a disappointing Wild Card series for the Chicago Cubs against the San Diego Padres, to say the least, and they were eventually swept.
The Cubs were unable to do anything on either side of the baseball for the better part of this series, with the offense being the biggest issue.
Chicago entered this Wild Card series with a chance to make some noise in the postseason, but the offense went absolutely quiet.
Expected National League MVP Award winner Pete Crow-Armstrong struggled just as much as anybody on the Cubs roster. Crow-Armstrong went 0-for-7 with four strikeouts, walking just once in the series, putting together a stolen base after that one walk.
Speaking to reporters after the game, the Cubs' 24-year-old superstar understands that he needed to be better, and while anybody can look at any numbers they want, it was obvious that he didn't contribute.
"We were challenged this year," Crow-Armstrong said, per The Athletic. "This team showed a lot of heart and a lot of fight through all the challenges. But I would say, to start: I show up. I show up when it matters in these games. That would help us immediately. But that's all I got right now."
"You can look at the scoreboard, you can look at the stat sheet, wherever you get your numbers from, and it is clear to see that I didn't contribute," Crow-Armstrong said.
Crow-Armstrong has never been the type of guy to beat around the bush and say he didn't do what was needed on both sides of the ball.
Unfortunately for the young man, this was a very disappointing series, one that he's going to have to live with throughout the remainder of the offseason. He had an incredible regular season, finishing the campaign with 45 home runs and a .943 OPS.
That wasn't even close to what he was able to do in the postseason.

item.title: [Yahoo Sports] Cubs Won't Get Into ‘Bidding War’ For Seiya Suzuki
item.dc:creator: Joey Pollizze
item.description: It didn't take long for free agent rumors to start swirling. The Chicago Cubs were just swept by the San Diego Padres in the National League Wild Card Round a few days ago, and free-agent rumors are already circling the baseball world. It will no doubt be a busy offseason for the Cubs, who have plenty of players hitting free agency. Players like Kevin Gausman, Shota Imanaga, David Peterson, and Carson Kelly will all test the open market this winter. However, the biggest question mark this offsea
item.content:encoded:
It didn't take long for free agent rumors to start swirling.
The Chicago Cubs were just swept by the San Diego Padres in the National League Wild Card Round a few days ago, and free-agent rumors are already circling the baseball world.
It will no doubt be a busy offseason for the Cubs, who have plenty of players hitting free agency. Players like Kevin Gausman, Shota Imanaga, David Peterson, and Carson Kelly will all test the open market this winter.
However, the biggest question mark this offseason for the Cubs is what they plan to do with their outfield. Both Ian Happ and Seiya Suzuki are free agents at the conclusion of this year's World Series. That leaves the team in a potential rough spot.
The Cubs have to answer one of these questions ahead of free agency:
- Do we bring back both Happ and Suzuki and simply run it back with the same outfield core?
- Do we pay Happ and let Suzuki walk, since he will cost much less?
- Do we pay Suzuki big money and let Happ walk because Suzuki gives us the best chance to win?
The front office will obviously weigh all these options ahead of free agency. However, it seems as if the Cubs have already made somewhat of a decision about Suzuki's future with the organization.
Patrick Mooney of The Athletic reported that "it's unlikely that the Cubs will get into a bidding war for Suzuki's services, let alone win one."
Hearing that the Cubs won't enter a bidding war for Suzuki doesn't bode well for their chances of getting him back. Teams like the Dodgers, Blue Jays, and Yankees are better suited to get into a bidding war for the slugger than the North Siders.
Mitch Bannon of the Athletic already reported that the Blue Jays will pursue Suzuki this offseason. Given that Toronto isn't afraid to spend on big-time players (e.g., Dylan Cease last offseason), there's a strong chance that the outfielder doesn't re-sign with the Cubs.
Losing Suzuki in free agency would be a big loss for the North Siders. He has been one of the team's best power hitters since the Cubs signed him out of Japan in 2022. The Japanese slugger has 113 home runs over his five MLB seasons and has 58 home runs with 189 RBI combined over the past two years.
The Cubs would be losing that power bat at the top of their lineup if he goes to another team. Unfortunately, it's very possible he does leave.

item.title: [Diario AS] Dodgers NLDS roster: Who will make the 26-man playoff roster against the Braves?
item.dc:creator: Rodrigo Serrano; Jennifer Bubel
item.description: The Los Angeles Dodgers have won the National League West for the fifth consecutive season and for the 13th time in the last 14 years. The only team to interrupt their run was the San Francisco Giants in 2021. Since then, no one has been able to take the division away from Los Angeles. item.content:encoded:
The Los Angeles Dodgers have won the National League West for the fifth consecutive season and for the 13th time in the last 14 years. The only team to interrupt their run was the San Francisco Giants in 2021. Since then, no one has been able to take the division away from Los Angeles.
Now the defending back-to-back World Series champions are preparing for the National League Division Series, where they will face the Atlanta Braves beginning Saturday at Dodger Stadium. Atlanta advanced by defeating the Philadelphia Phillies in the Wild Card Series, setting up the Dodgers’ first postseason matchup with the Braves since the 2021 NL Championship Series.
Your 2026 Los Angeles Dodgers. pic.twitter.com/XYs9LzjRIb
— Los Angeles Dodgers (@Dodgers) September 24, 2026
The Dodgers’ five-day bye gave Dave Roberts and his staff time to prepare their roster, and while most of the pieces are already in place, there are still some important decisions to make before the 26-man NLDS roster is finalized. MLB reports that the final bench spot remains particularly unsettled, while the bullpen could also have an opening depending on the health of Edgardo Henriquez.
Who will make the Dodgers’ pitching staff?
The Dodgers’ biggest strength heading into October is their starting rotation. Yoshinobu Yamamoto, Tarik Skubal, Blake Snell, and Tyler Glasnow form a formidable group, although Roberts had not formally announced the order entering Friday.
Yamamoto is the leading candidate to start Game 1 against Atlanta. His normal rest schedule is one of the reasons the Japanese right-hander makes the most sense for the opener, as starting Saturday would also give him the chance to be available for a potential Game 5 on his usual rest.
#ITFDB presented by Toyo Tires. pic.twitter.com/TcKpliJrnR
— Los Angeles Dodgers (@Dodgers) September 24, 2026
The Dodgers also have several pitchers who could be used in relief despite spending much of the regular season as starters. Roki Sasaki, Justin Wrobleski and Emmet Sheehan are among the options who could give Roberts additional flexibility out of the bullpen.
Edgardo Henriquez is another name to watch. The right-hander emerged as an important leverage option during the regular season before lower back discomfort ended his year prematurely. The Dodgers planned to have him face hitters during the bye, with an activation for the NLDS possible if he comes through the workout without any problems.
What will the Dodgers’ offense look like?
Shohei Ohtani will once again be the centerpiece of the Dodgers’ offense, but the situation is different from what it appeared to be when the original story was written.
Ohtani returned from the injured list in late September and played in each of the Dodgers’ final five regular-season games. He went 5-for-21 with eight strikeouts and one walk during that stretch, but Roberts said the team had no health concerns with its superstar heading into the postseason.
It’s Shotime! On this day in 2024, Shohei Ohtani started the 50/50 club.
This MomenTito’s in Dodger history presented by Tito's Handmade Vodka. pic.twitter.com/cxOEcJyPNK
— Los Angeles Dodgers (@Dodgers) September 19, 2026
Ohtani is expected to remain the designated hitter, with Mookie Betts at shortstop, Freddie Freeman at first base and Max Muncy at third. The Dodgers’ outfield is also largely established, with Kyle Tucker, Teoscar Hernández and Andy Pages expected to occupy the three spots.
The lineup could continue to feature some adjustments depending on the opposing starter. Against right-handed pitching, Ohtani has been used at the top of the order, while Betts has taken the leadoff spot against left-handers. That platoon is expected to continue into October.
Who's your Player of the Game? Comment your answer below! pic.twitter.com/tt6sVtGvWT
— Los Angeles Dodgers (@Dodgers) September 26, 2026
Who gets the final roster spot?
The Dodgers have several candidates competing for what could be their final bench spot: Josue De Paula, Dalton Rushing, Alex Call, and Hyeseong Kim. MLB’s postseason preview identified the decision as one of the biggest remaining questions for the club.
De Paula is intriguing after his impressive first taste of the Majors. The Dodgers’ top prospect hit .323 with seven RBIs and seven runs scored in 11 games before being optioned to Triple-A when Ohtani returned from the injured list. His performance was strong enough to keep him in the postseason conversation.
But Kim offers something different. His defensive versatility, speed, and ability to contribute off the bench could make him valuable in a playoff series, particularly if Roberts wants another defensive option late in games.
MLB.com Dodgers beat reporter Sonja Chen noted that both De Paula and Kim could have a chance to make the NLDS roster if Los Angeles carries 14 position players and 12 pitchers. The final decision could ultimately come down to whether the Dodgers prefer another impact bat or additional speed and defense.
Rushing and Call remain possibilities as well, meaning the Dodgers have not simply decided between De Paula and Kim.
The other variable is the pitching staff. If Los Angeles carries only 12 pitchers rather than the maximum 13, it would open another position-player spot and potentially allow Roberts to keep more of those candidates.
Dodgers are chasing history
There is plenty more than a division title at stake for Los Angeles. The Dodgers are attempting to become the first team since the New York Yankees from 1998-2000 to win three consecutive World Series titles. They have already won three of the past six championships and enter October as the defending champions for the second straight year.
Their first obstacle is now set: the Atlanta Braves. The two teams will meet Saturday in Game 1 of the NLDS at Dodger Stadium, with Yamamoto the likely starter for Los Angeles. Before the first pitch, however, Roberts and the Dodgers still have a handful of decisions to make about exactly which players will be part of their attempt at a historic three-peat.

item.content:encoded:
Ranking Phillies 2B Luis Arraez's Top 5 Landing Spots Ahead of MLB Free Agency
Any club pursuing three-time batting champion Luis Arraez will likely need a plan to play him regularly at second base.
In a 2026 season split between the San Francisco Giants and Philadelphia Phillies, Arraez returned to his natural position of second base. In terms of outs above average, he had the best season of his career, with San Francisco infield coach Ron Washington credited with helping his defensive growth.
Arraez should do better this offseason than the one-year, $12 million deal he settled for last offseason. He was unavailable for the Phillies' Wild Card Series loss to Atlanta because of a sprained left ankle, though the injury is not expected to affect his availability for 2027.
Let's take a look at the best potential landing spots for the four-time All-Star.
5. Texas Rangers
1 of 5
Whether the Rangers are in on Arraez will depend on whether managing partner Ray Davis authorizes president of baseball operations Chris Young to add payroll in the offseason.
From a baseball perspective, the Rangers' second basemen posted an OPS south of .700 this season. Clearly, Arraez would give them more offensively than they got in 2026.
Top prospect Sebastian Walcott is a shortstop/third baseman who is expected to play a role for the team in 2027. But even with Corey Seager at shortstop and Josh Jung at third base, Walcott seems more likely to play outfield than second base. There aren't many 6'4" second basemen.
4. Philadelphia Phillies
2 of 5
Arraez didn't perform as well with the Phillies as he did with the Giants, but his track record suggests that over a larger sample size, he will hit for a higher average.
The Phillies dealt pitching prospects Ramon Marquez and Marty Gair to acquire Arraez and reliever Caleb Kilian, so they should at least consider a reunion in free agency.
That said, some of this will come down to how the Phillies want to set up their infield in 2027. Alec Bohm will likely depart in free agency, while Bryce Harper is expected to return to first base.
Will the Phillies move Trea Turner off of shortstop, and if so will that be to second base or left field? What about Bryson Stott, whom the team likes at second base but moved to third to accommodate Arraez? Also looming is top prospect Aidan Miller, who missed most of 2026 but is an exciting bat who can play shortstop or third base.
Many moving parts make it unclear whether the Phillies will commit to multiple seasons of Arraez at second base. Still, his presence behind Bryce Harper gave Philadelphia a contact-oriented option in the heart of its lineup and may have made it easier for Harper to remain selective at the plate.
3. Pittsburgh Pirates
3 of 5
Will the Pirates extend the qualifying offer to Brandon Lowe? It's always difficult to know how owner Bob Nutting will operate. Even if the QO goes to Lowe, one would think he'd decline it in search of a multi-year commitment.
If Lowe ends up not returning to Pittsburgh, the Buccos will have a hole at second base. One way to soften the negative reaction to not bringing Lowe back after an excellent contract year is to sign a replacement as accomplished as Arraez.
You could do worse than a middle-infield pairing of Arraez and Konnor Griffin, especially in terms of offensive production.
2. San Francisco Giants
4 of 5
It's rare but not unheard of for a player to get traded midseason and then return to the club that traded him in the offseason as a free agent. This might be one of the instances where it makes sense, though.
Arraez not only built a great relationship with the aforementioned Washington, but he also hit .324 in 105 games with the Giants. While home run hitters other than Barry Bonds don't love Oracle Park, Arraez's offensive profile fit the park well. In 49 games at Oracle Park in 2026, Arraez hit .361.
This may come down to whether the Giants are comfortable with Casey Schmitt playing elsewhere on the diamond so Arraez can resume as the team's second baseman. Offensively, Arraez remains a great fit for the Giants.
1. Detroit Tigers
5 of 5
The Tigers will have quite a bit of money coming off the books this offseason, including the $22.025 million that Gleyber Torres made after accepting the qualifying offer last winter.
Arraez spent the first four seasons of his career with the Minnesota Twins, so a return to the AL Central could make sense. It's a bit surprising that Arraez has hit only .265 in 88 career plate appearances at Comerica Park, but the spacious outfield suits a contact hitter.
Additionally, with Torres coming off the books, the Tigers will have an opening at second base. Adding Arraez's bat-to-ball skills could help Detroit rebound from a disappointing 2026.

item.title: [Yahoo Sports] Cubs’ Dansby Swanson Says Goodbye To 4-Time Gold Glove Teammate After Brutal Exit
item.dc:creator: Peter Chawaga; Contributor
item.description: The Chicago Cubs entered the 2026 postseason with legitimate expectations of making another deep October run. Instead, their season ended abruptly in San Diego, leaving the organization to confront a disappointing Wild Card exit and some difficult questions about what comes next. item.content:encoded:
The Chicago Cubs entered the 2026 postseason with legitimate expectations of making another deep October run. Instead, their season ended abruptly in San Diego, leaving the organization to confront a disappointing Wild Card exit and some difficult questions about what comes next.
The Cubs were swept by the San Diego Padres in the National League Wild Card Series, falling 4-1 in Wednesday's decisive game at Petco Park. The loss ended a season in which Chicago returned to the playoffs for a second consecutive year, but it also brought the future of several important veterans into sharper focus.
Among them is Ian Happ, the longest-tenured player on Chicago's active roster and a four-time Gold Glove winner in left field.
"Happ was drafted by the Cubs in the 2015 MLB Draft and has spent his entire professional career with the Cubs ever since," Alex Dvorak noted for NBC 5 Chicago. "But he is expected to become a free agent in 2027, leaving his future with the team uncertain."
After the loss, franchise shortstop Dansby Swanson offered an emotional assessment of what Happ has meant to the Cubs and to him personally.
Chicago Cubs Star Dansby Swanson Reflects On Ian Happ's Cubs Legacy After Exit
With Happ potentially ending his Cubs career with a brutal postseason sweep, Swanson was asked immediately after the game what his teammate has meant to him.
"That's a tough one," Swanson said, getting noticeably choked up in a clubhouse interview with Marquee Sports Network. "He's meant a lot to me. I think he truly embodies what it means to wear the jersey."
Happ debuted with the Cubs in 2017 and developed into an established veteran, earning an All-Star selection in 2022 and four consecutive Gold Glove Awards from 2022 through 2025.
That defensive consistency became one part of Happ's identity in Chicago, but his importance to the organization extends beyond his production. He has been through multiple versions of the Cubs and remained a fixture as the franchise rebuilt around a younger core.
Swanson, who joined Chicago before the 2023 season, clearly developed a particularly close relationship with Happ.
"He's probably my longest friend that I've had here, so yeah, that probably speaks enough for itself," Swanson added. "He embodies the Cubs more than anyone I know so he's a big reason why I'm here and I'm very thankful for him."
Chicago Cubs Face Ian Happ Decision After Playoff Exit
Following the unceremonious playoff exit, Happ is now among the Cubs players whose futures could become a significant offseason storyline, meaning Wednesday's loss may have been the final game of his Chicago tenure.
That possibility helps explain the emotion surrounding Swanson's comments. Happ has become closely associated with the Cubs since entering the organization as a first-round pick, and his potential departure would remove one of the most familiar faces from a clubhouse that just experienced another disappointing postseason ending.
After a season that ended far earlier than Chicago hoped, Swanson's goodbye captured the significance of the franchise's longest-tenured players.
This article was originally published on Forbes.com

item.title: [FanSided] MLB Power Rankings: Every remaining playoff team after Wild Card Round
item.dc:creator: Christopher Kline
